control: AI security policy and acceptable use
requirement: A published AI security policy states which AI services are sanctioned and the data classes each may process (by reference to the approved AI catalog, BAL-8.10), prohibited uses, rules for ambient-capture AI such as meeting notetakers and screen recall, the maximum autonomy level permitted for each use type, and the approvals each asset risk rating requires. Users acknowledge it before first use and after material change. It is reviewed at least annually and after material change in AI use, threats or applicable law.
evidence: Approved AI security policy with version history and last review date; acknowledgement records for a sample of users, including recent joiners; the policy sections mapping use types to maximum autonomy levels and risk ratings to approval routes.
guidance: Point the policy at living artifacts, such as the BAL-8.10 catalog and the tiering guide, so it does not go stale. Ambient-capture rules usually cover auto-joining meetings with external participants, participant notice and consent where law requires it, where summaries and transcripts go, and screen-history features on managed devices. Comparable requirement: AIUC-1 E010 (AI acceptable use policy).

control: AI security roles and decision rights
requirement: Named roles hold the decision rights to approve autonomy promotions (BAL-3.1), exceptions and risk acceptances at each asset risk rating (BAL-1.13), and production release of High and Critical assets (BAL-1.6, BAL-5.6), and a named AI security incident lead is assigned. Changes to AI policy, guardrails and agent configuration are approved by someone other than their author. AI platform administration is held by roles separate from those that build or publish agents.
evidence: Decision-rights matrix naming the role and current holder for each approval type and risk rating, including the AI security incident lead; a sample of policy, guardrail and agent-configuration changes showing an approver other than the author; AI platform role assignments showing administrators and agent makers are separate.
guidance: Ballast does not prescribe a governance forum; map these rights onto the existing AI governance body or ISO/IEC 42001 clause 5.3 roles. Scale authority with risk, for example a security architect for Medium, the CISO for High, and an executive risk owner for Critical assets and any A4 authorization. BAL-5.2 enforces two-person change approval for built assets; BAL-6.17 configures platform roles.

control: AI security awareness and role-based training
requirement: People who use, build, approve or operate AI receive AI security training matched to their role, covering at least prompt injection and untrusted content, permitted data handling, verifying AI output and, for people who approve agent actions, automation bias. Agent makers, developers of AI assets, approvers, AI administrators and security operations staff complete it before the role is granted; other users complete it within a defined period of first access; everyone repeats it at least annually. Completion is recorded.
evidence: Role-to-curriculum matrix with content outlines; completion records for a sample of makers, approvers and AI administrators showing training finished before the role was granted; report of users past the defined first-access period without completion.
guidance: Suggested default: 30 days from first access for general users. Cover deepfakes and AI-enabled social engineering through the general awareness programme, as the NYDFS October 2024 AI letter expects. Supports EU AI Act Art. 4 (AI literacy, applying since 2 Feb 2025) and ETSI EN 304 223 provision 5.1.1-1; the UK NCSC (Dec 2025) lists awareness first among its prompt-injection mitigations.

requirement: Every AI asset has a named, accountable human owner assigned at registration, and ownership is transferred or removed only through a defined lifecycle. On transfer, grants and connections that run under the previous owner's personal credentials are re-issued under a dedicated agent identity (BAL-2.1) or, for an assistant that acts only for its owner, under the new owner. Assets whose owner leaves or changes role are identified from joiner-mover-leaver events and are re-owned, suspended or decommissioned (BAL-1.15) within a defined period.
evidence: Register extract showing an accountable owner for every asset; joiner-mover-leaver feed matched against asset owners, with resulting re-ownership or suspension tickets and closure times; one recent ownership transfer showing grants moved off the previous owner's credentials.
guidance: Suggested default: re-own, suspend or retire within 30 days of the owner leaving or changing role. The owner answers for the asset's rating, exceptions and retirement. Agent identities also have a sponsor under BAL-2.2, who may be the same person. Automated detection of agents running on a person's credentials is BAL-2.9 (T2).

control: AI asset risk rating and capability profile
requirement: Each AI asset is rated Low, Medium, High or Critical with the Ballast rubric from its reach, exposure, access, agency and consequential use, and its record lists its capability tags, its autonomy level for each action class, its initiation mode and its hosting model (organization-operated, vendor-operated or built on a vendor platform). It is at least High if it can reach restricted or regulated data; has any action class at A3 or above or carries the EXEC tag; meets the untrusted-input combination of BAL-3.5 or has external users (PUBLIC); or makes or materially supports consequential decisions about individuals or is high-risk under applicable AI law. It is Critical if any action class is at A4, or if that consequential-use condition holds together with the autonomy-or-execution or untrusted-input condition. The rating sets the applicable Control Tiers, approval workflow and review cadence, and is re-assessed on material change.
evidence: Completed rubric for a sample of assets showing inputs, capability tags, autonomy level per action class, initiation mode and resulting rating; register report of assets by rating and applicable Control Tiers; re-rating records triggered by recent material changes.
guidance: Restricted data means the organization's highest classes (for example health, payment card or special-category personal data, secrets, privileged systems), not merely internal or client-confidential data. Event-triggered initiation by external content counts as untrusted input. The BAL-3.5 untrusted-input profile is recorded with the rating. The Low/Medium split is organization-defined; both get T1, High adds T2, and Critical adds T2 with T3 recommended (required at A4). Full rubric: guides/tiering.md.

requirement: No AI application, agent, model or newly enabled AI feature reaches production users or production data, including pilots that use real data, identities or credentials, until it is registered in the AI asset register with its owner (BAL-1.4), intended purpose, data classes, autonomy level per action class and risk rating (BAL-1.5), and is approved through the workflow its rating requires. A material change is re-registered and re-approved before release. A vendor-enabled feature that cannot be held off is detected through BAL-1.10 and brought into intake within a defined period or excepted under BAL-1.13. An agent used only by its maker inside a registered low-code builder is covered by the builder's registration (BAL-1.11).
evidence: Intake workflow with approval routes per risk rating; for a sample of recent assets and material changes, register entries whose approval dates precede first production use; vendor-enabled features found under BAL-1.10 with their intake or exception dates.
guidance: Material change includes a new model or model version, a new tool or action class, a new data source or data class, a new user population, or a higher autonomy level. Discovery controls (BAL-1.8, 1.9, 1.10, 8.9) find what bypassed intake and route it back here. Suggested default: vendor-enabled features enter intake within 30 days of detection.

requirement: Each AI application and agent the organization builds or configures has an AI bill of materials recording its models (provider, model identifier and version or snapshot, hosting region, model documentation and applicable terms), agents and sub-agents, skills and plugins, MCP servers and tools, agent frameworks and SDKs (including MCP SDKs), retrieval sources and indexes, and the owner of each component. The AI bill of materials is updated at each release and material change.
evidence: AI bills of materials for a sample of built assets, with model identifiers and versions matching the deployed configuration; release records showing the AI BOM updated with each change; component owners resolvable to current staff.
guidance: CycloneDX ML-BOM (version 1.5 and later) and the SPDX 3.0 AI profile are suitable, non-mandatory formats; generating the BOM from deployment manifests keeps it accurate. Recording agent-framework and MCP SDK versions lets advisories be matched to assets. Training-data and weight lineage for models the organization trains or fine-tunes is BAL-5.15 (T2). Vendor-operated AI features are inventoried under BAL-1.10 instead.

control: Model and AI provider usage inventory
requirement: Every model endpoint, AI provider account, project and API key in use, whether provider-hosted, cloud-hosted or self-hosted, is recorded with its consuming application or identity, its owner and its hosting region. The record is reconciled at least quarterly against billing and cloud-resource records and, where an AI gateway is used, gateway records, and model use that is not registered is routed to intake (BAL-1.6).
evidence: Inventory of provider accounts, projects, API keys and model endpoints with consuming application, owner and region; the latest quarterly reconciliation against invoices, cloud resource listings and gateway records; intake tickets raised for unregistered use it found.
guidance: Reconciliation should surface keys created by departed staff, subscriptions paid on personal cards and models deployed in unapproved regions. Self-hosted inference endpoints recorded here are hardened under BAL-6.19; usage and spend ceilings are BAL-3.8. In a September 2026 case reported by Unit 42, intruders used the victim's own AI endpoints with stolen cloud keys.

requirement: AI agents and assistants, command-line coding agents, local model runtimes, local MCP servers, AI-enabled IDE and browser extensions, and AI browsers on managed endpoints are discovered on a defined cadence and recorded with version, install source, last-active time, user and device.
evidence: Discovery job definitions covering each listed category, with run history at the defined cadence; current endpoint AI inventory with version, install source, last-active time, user and device; tickets raised for discovered unapproved items.
guidance: Suggested default: daily collection from endpoint management or EDR software inventory, plus scans of agent and IDE configuration files for locally defined MCP servers; include OS and browser screen-recall features. In August 2025 the s1ngularity (Nx) malware ran locally installed AI coding CLIs with permission-bypass flags to hunt for secrets. Findings feed the approved component catalog (BAL-5.18), configuration lockdown (BAL-6.16) and shadow-AI response (BAL-8.10).

requirement: AI features embedded in approved SaaS applications are inventoried per tenant with their activation scope (tenant, group or user), the data classes they can reach, and whether memory or personalization is enabled. Where the platform allows it, new or default-on AI features stay disabled until approved through BAL-1.6.
evidence: Per-tenant inventory of embedded AI features with activation scope, reachable data classes and memory status; admin-console settings showing new or default-on features disabled pending approval; intake records for features enabled since the last review.
guidance: Vendor notices of new or changed AI features are monitored under BAL-8.8, which feeds this inventory; tenant security settings, including meeting-recap and notetaker features, are baselined under BAL-6.17. Example: Microsoft documents that Anthropic models are on by default in Microsoft 365 Copilot for most commercial-cloud customers outside the EU/EFTA and UK.

requirement: In the low-code and end-user agent builders the organization offers, agent creation is limited to authorized makers, an agent is registered under BAL-1.6 before it is shared beyond its maker or given access to data or actions beyond the maker's own, and sharing with broad audiences, such as the whole organization or external users, requires approval. An agent used only by its maker is covered by the builder platform's registration and its BAL-6.17 baseline. Shared agents do not run on the maker's personal credentials (BAL-2.1).
evidence: Builder settings restricting agent creation to an authorized-maker group and limiting sharing; for a sample of shared agents, register entries, approvals for organization-wide or external sharing, and connection settings showing no maker-provided personal credentials.
guidance: Some platforms allow unlimited sharing unless a limit is configured: Microsoft Copilot Studio sharing limits are a Managed Environments control and apply only to agents that require authentication. Maker-provided credentials let every user of a shared agent act with the maker's access, so use per-user authentication or a dedicated agent identity. Third-party app consent is BAL-2.6; platform-wide sharing settings are baselined in BAL-6.17.

requirement: Each AI asset's register entry records the jurisdictions and the AI-specific or sector rules that apply, the organization's role under them (for example provider or deployer), whether the asset makes or materially supports consequential decisions about individuals, and whether a data protection impact assessment or record of processing is required and where it is held. Obligations outside security, such as fairness and performance validation, transparency to affected people and human-oversight design, are assigned to a named AI governance or model-risk owner, who receives the asset's security test results where they exist (BAL-5.3, BAL-5.6).
evidence: Register entries for a sample of assets showing jurisdictions, applicable rules, provider or deployer role, consequential-decision flag and DPIA reference; named governance or model-risk owner for each consequential-use asset; record of security test results shared with that owner.
guidance: Consequential-decision use feeds the High and Critical rules in BAL-1.5. Examples: the EU AI Act lists creditworthiness and life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing as high-risk (Annex III, applying from 2 Dec 2027 after the 2026 AI Omnibus); Art. 50 transparency applies from 2 Aug 2026; NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7 (2024) and the NAIC model bulletin govern insurers' AI use. ISO/IEC 42005:2025 guides impact assessment.

requirement: Exceptions to Ballast controls, including deviations that other controls route here, are recorded in a central register with the control, the affected assets, residual risk, compensating controls, risk-register reference, an approver at the authority BAL-1.2 assigns to the asset's risk rating, and an expiry date. A T2 control may be tailored, meaning replaced by a documented compensating control that addresses the same risk, for at most 12 months. Risk acceptances last at most 6 months for High or Critical assets and 12 months otherwise, and may be renewed once, only with a funded remediation plan. Renew tailoring only with fresh approval and current evidence for the compensating control. Record A4 authorizations separately from control gaps, for at most 6 months, renewed only through a new promotion gate (BAL-3.1). Expired tailoring and risk acceptances revert to open gaps. A4 operation must stop when its authorization expires. Non-acceptable controls and the required T2/T3 controls for A4 assets cannot be tailored or risk-accepted. The register is reviewed at least quarterly.
evidence: Central register identifying T2 tailoring, risk acceptance or A4 authorization, with control, affected assets, residual risk, compensating controls, risk-register reference, approver and expiry; samples showing authority, durations and renewals within the applicable rules; A4 authorization linked to the approved action classes and promotion gate; quarterly review records showing expired tailoring and risk acceptances reopened as gaps and expired A4 operation stopped.
guidance: Only T2 controls may be replaced by approved compensating controls. Report them as 'with T2 tailoring,' separately from implemented coverage. Risk acceptance leaves a gap and is reported as Risk-accepted, never as conformant. Not applicable is derived from capability tags and needs no exception. Record T2 tailoring, risk acceptance or A4 authorization in the register. Link A4's approved action classes and promotion gate through the BAL-3.1 assessment's evidence, notes and exception_id fields; an authorization does not make a satisfied control Excepted. Other controls route deviations here, for example wildcard or administrative scopes (BAL-3.4), code-executing model loads (BAL-5.13) and internet exposure of self-hosted AI services (BAL-6.19).

requirement: Key risk indicators for AI security are reported to the accountable executive at a defined cadence, covering at least inventory completeness, T1 conformance by asset risk rating, agents by highest autonomy level, overdue and expiring exceptions, the trend in unsanctioned AI use, and AI security incidents.
evidence: The last two KRI reports to the accountable executive, dated at the defined cadence; definitions and data sources for each indicator; decisions or actions recorded when an indicator breached its threshold.
guidance: Suggested default: quarterly to the accountable executive, with an annual summary to the board. Inventory completeness can be measured as the share of assets found by discovery (BAL-1.8, 1.9, 1.10, 8.9) that were already registered. Useful additions: approval volume and time-to-decide (BAL-3.12) and A3-or-higher agents with a tested kill switch (BAL-3.7).

requirement: When an AI asset is retired, its identities, credentials, OAuth grants and consents, role bindings, connectors, and MCP and tool registrations are revoked; its endpoints, published interfaces, triggers and webhooks are removed; its weights, fine-tunes, embeddings, indexes, memory, prompts and configuration are deleted or archived under BAL-4.4; deletion of its vendor-held data is requested and confirmed (BAL-8.3); and its register entry is closed with evidence that no residual access remains.
evidence: Decommissioning checklist for a recently retired asset with each step signed off; identity-provider and cloud IAM queries showing no bindings, grants or consents still referencing its identities; vendor deletion confirmation where vendor-held data existed.
guidance: Retirement often leaves access behind: Google Cloud documents that deleting an Agent Engine agent does not remove IAM bindings that reference its principal; they must be removed manually. Agent identities retire through BAL-2.2, third-party AI grants through BAL-2.7, and legal hold overrides deletion (BAL-4.4). Triggers, schedules and sub-agents recorded under BAL-3.7 show what else must be switched off.

requirement: Each agent that acts under its own credentials has a dedicated non-human identity whose permissions are limited to what its registered purpose requires (BAL-1.6). No credential is shared between agents or between an agent and a person, and an agent does not use any person's credentials, including its maker's, to act for other users. Agent identities used in development, test or experimental contexts hold no production write access. Static secrets are used only where the target supports no stronger method, and are then governed by BAL-2.4.
evidence: Identity-provider or platform export mapping each agent identity to a registered agent; sample of agent connections and connectors showing no shared, personal or maker-provided credentials; role assignments of non-production agent identities showing no production write access
guidance: An agent that acts only for its invoking user is assessed under BAL-2.3. Prefer platform workload identity to static keys. Where a SaaS platform cannot issue a distinct agent principal, a dedicated least-privilege integration account per agent meets this control. A shared admin, shared integration or personal account does not, and needs a BAL-1.13 exception. Replit (Jul 2025): after its agent deleted a production database, Replit separated development and production databases.

requirement: Every agent identity has a named human sponsor, recorded in the organization's identity governance process, who is accountable for its access. The identity's access is certified at a cadence set by the asset's risk rating (BAL-1.5). When the sponsor leaves or changes role, the identity is reassigned to a new sponsor or disabled within a defined period. An identity that is no longer needed is retired under BAL-1.15, with removal of its credentials, grants and role bindings verified at each target.
evidence: Register of agent identities with sponsor, risk rating and last certification date; certification records for a sample of identities checked against the required cadence; leaver or mover test showing an identity reassigned or disabled within the defined period
guidance: Suggested defaults: certify quarterly for High or Critical assets and annually otherwise; reassign or disable within 5 business days of a sponsor's departure. The sponsor can be the asset's owner of record (BAL-1.4), and one joiner-mover-leaver process can serve both. Some platforms keep role bindings as inactive grants after an agent is deleted (Google Cloud agent identity documentation), so verify removal at the resource. Informative: OWASP NHI Top 10 NHI1.

requirement: When an agent acts for a user, each downstream request carries verifiable identities of both the user (subject) and the agent (actor) and is authorized against the intersection of their permissions. The credential used is audience-bound under BAL-3.4 and is valid only for that task, up to a defined maximum lifetime. An agent serving several users authorizes each request against the user who made it and does not forward the user's upstream token to another service. Requests that claim to act for a user but lack verifiable user context are denied. A single-user assistant that acts only for its own user, within that user's session and under that user's own credentials, meets this control when it holds no credentials beyond the user's and the enforcement point records its actions as the assistant's (BAL-7.1).
evidence: For delegated credentials: token or target-system log samples showing user and agent identities, audience and lifetime, with token-exchange configuration where applicable. For the single-user route: enforcement-point logs identifying the assistant's actions and evidence that it acts only for that user with no additional credentials. Negative tests show unauthorized access, requests without required user context and cross-user use are denied.
guidance: Examples: OAuth 2.0 token exchange (RFC 8693) or on-behalf-of flows. A user ID in a header or prompt is not verifiable. Suggested maximum lifetime: 1 hour. Prefer credentials issued specifically to the assistant. A single-user assistant may use its user's session only when it acts solely for that user, has no additional credentials, and its actions are identifiable in enforcement-point logs. Other credential and isolation controls still apply. Actions under the agent's own identity are attributed to its sponsor (BAL-2.2). Content from other users can still steer the agent (BAL-3.5).

control: Agent credential storage, lifetime and revocation
requirement: Agent credentials, including those used by MCP servers, plugins and connectors, are held only in an approved secret store or issued at runtime through platform workload identity. They are not placed in prompts, model context, memory, code, logs or agent and MCP configuration files, and those files are scanned for plaintext credentials. Each credential has an enforced maximum lifetime set by the asset's risk rating. Revocation takes effect at every relying party within a defined objective, through continuous access evaluation or token lifetimes no longer than that objective, and is tested at least annually.
evidence: Secret-scanning results covering agent, MCP and plugin configuration files and sampled prompts, memory and logs; credential inventory showing issuer, maximum lifetime and expiry for each agent credential; latest revocation test with time to denial at each relying party
guidance: Suggested defaults: access tokens 1 hour or less; no non-expiring keys without a BAL-1.13 exception; revocation within 15 minutes, matching the BAL-3.7 halt objective. Shared Signals and CAEP events, or short token lifetimes, carry revocation to relying parties. The IETF AIMS draft (work in progress) calls static API keys an antipattern. Vaulting does not protect credentials in use (Unit 42, Sep 2026); see BAL-6.13 and BAL-2.11.

requirement: Human access to sanctioned AI services uses enterprise single sign-on with conditional access. Accounts on those services are provisioned automatically from the enterprise identity source and deprovisioned within a defined period of a person leaving. Agent identities are issued by, or federated to, the enterprise identity provider wherever the target system supports it; otherwise the agent's credentials are governed by BAL-2.4.
evidence: List of sanctioned AI services showing single sign-on, conditional-access policy and provisioning method for each; leaver test showing AI service accounts, keys and tokens disabled within the defined period; list of agent identities with their issuing or federated identity provider
guidance: For example SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect with SCIM; suggested deprovisioning within 24 hours of departure. Disable local password sign-in where the service allows it. Confirm that deprovisioning also revokes API keys and tokens the leaver created on AI platforms (BAL-1.8). The MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension, built on the IETF ID-JAG draft, lets the identity provider decide which AI clients may reach which MCP servers.

requirement: Users can connect third-party AI apps, connectors, meeting notetakers and agents to organizational accounts or data only after an administrator approves the app, following a least-privilege review of the scopes it requests. User self-consent to unapproved apps is disabled on every identity provider and SaaS platform that supports disabling it.
evidence: Consent settings from each identity provider and SaaS platform showing user self-consent disabled or limited to approved apps; sample of AI app approval records with scope review and approver; list of platforms that cannot restrict consent, with the compensating control
guidance: The Vercel incident (Apr 2026) originated with the compromise of Context.ai, a third-party AI tool used by an employee and connected as a Google Workspace OAuth app (Vercel bulletin). Identity providers rarely distinguish AI apps, so this usually means admin consent for all third-party apps, with AI apps routed through intake (BAL-1.6). Where self-consent cannot be disabled, BAL-2.7 and BAL-8.9 find the resulting grants.

control: Third-party AI grant inventory and revocation
requirement: Every OAuth grant, refresh token, API key and connected-app authorization held by a third-party AI app or vendor is inventoried with its internal owner, scopes and reachable data. Each is recertified at a cadence set by the app's risk rating (BAL-1.5). Where the platform supports it, each grant is restricted to the vendor's network ranges or tenant. All grants held by one vendor can be revoked across every platform within a defined objective, and this revocation is exercised at least annually.
evidence: Per-vendor grant inventory listing platform, owner, scopes, reachable data and last recertification; platform settings showing network-range or tenant restrictions where supported; record of the latest per-vendor revocation exercise with platforms covered and elapsed time
guidance: In August 2025, attackers used OAuth tokens held by Salesloft's Drift AI chat integration to export data from customers' Salesforce instances, and used Drift Email tokens against Google Workspace (GTIG); Salesloft then revoked all tokens. Suggested defaults: recertify quarterly for High or Critical apps and annually otherwise; per-vendor revocation within 4 hours. Bulk export by these identities is detected under BAL-7.5 where implemented.

control: MCP server authentication and token audience
requirement: Every remote MCP server the organization operates, or approves for non-public data or write-capable tools, authenticates every request, accepts only tokens issued for that server and forwards no received token to other services. Unauthenticated remote servers are approved only for public data and read-only tools. MCP clients the organization operates or approves validate the authorization server's issuer and send each token only to the server it was issued for. Conformance with the current MCP authorization specification is checked at approval and whenever the specification revision or SDK version in use changes.
evidence: Per-server tests showing that an unauthenticated request and a token issued for another audience are both rejected; client configuration or test showing issuer validation and per-server token use; approval records naming the MCP specification revision and SDK versions checked
guidance: MCP specification 2026-07-28: servers publish Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) and validate audience; clients send resource indicators (RFC 8707) and validate issuer (RFC 9207); token passthrough is forbidden. A May 2026 study found 40.55% of 7,973 remote MCP servers exposed tools without authentication (arXiv 2605.22333). GHSA-qx49-fqc8-xw99 (MCP Python SDK, Sep 2026) is why SDK changes trigger a re-check. Local servers: prefer stdio; bind HTTP servers to loopback and validate Origin (BAL-6.16).

control: Agent identity hygiene and misuse detection
requirement: Agent identities and grants that are unused, or that hold permissions not exercised, over a defined period are detected and removed or reduced within a defined time. Interactive sign-in by a person using an agent identity is blocked, or alerted where the platform cannot block it. Agents that serve other users while running on one person's personal or maker-provided credentials are detected and either moved to a dedicated identity (BAL-2.1) or disabled.
evidence: Report of granted versus used permissions per agent identity, with remediation tickets; sign-in policy or alert rule for interactive use of agent identities, with a test result; detection results for agents running on personal or maker-provided credentials, with their resolution
guidance: Suggested defaults: 90 days unused or unexercised; remediation within 30 days. Human use of an agent identity breaks attribution (OWASP NHI Top 10 NHI10, informative). Some low-code builders offer maker-provided credentials as a connection option. This control finds such connections serving other users; BAL-1.11 is the preventive control. Grants held by third-party AI apps are recertified under BAL-2.7.

requirement: Agents hold no standing privilege for sensitive operations: administrative or privileged access, secret retrieval or privileged credential use, permission, access or credential changes, changes to security controls or monitoring, and production changes (BAL-3.6). These privileges are granted as short-lived credentials scoped to the specific task, minted at the time of use, and expire or are revoked when the task ends. Any justification or ticket reference needed to obtain them comes from the invoking person or workflow system, not from model-generated text.
evidence: Role assignments showing no standing administrative or privileged roles for agent identities; issuance logs showing task-scoped credentials, their lifetimes and revocation at task end; configuration showing that justification is taken from the ticket or workflow system
guidance: For example token exchange or workload identity federation that mints a credential per task, or rich authorization requests (RFC 9396) that describe the transaction. Suggested default: privileged credentials expire within 15 minutes. Once untrusted content is in context, an attacker can steer a model-written justification. CoSAI Agentic IAM v1.0 (Mar 2026) recommends short-lived delegation tokens and zero standing privilege. Scope limits are BAL-3.4.

requirement: Credentials used by an asset tagged EXEC are attached to its outbound requests by a broker, gateway or proxy that runs outside any execution context the model can direct, so the agent's shell, code and file tools cannot read, print or export them. No usable credential is present in environment variables, files or process memory reachable from those tools.
evidence: Architecture showing the credential broker outside every model-directed execution context; negative tests through each available code, shell or filesystem-writing tool showing usable credentials cannot be read or exported from environment variables, files or process memory; broker logs showing per-request credential injection.
guidance: Unit 42 (Sep 2026) read a vaulted service-account JWT from an AWS AgentCore Harness process's memory through its default shell tool, then replayed it from an outside laptop. Vaults protect credentials at rest and in transit, not in use. CI steps that expose secrets to agents as environment variables fail the same way. Typical patterns: an egress proxy or MCP gateway that adds authorization headers, or a sidecar token broker. Builds on BAL-6.13.

requirement: When delegation passes through more than one agent or service, each hop obtains a new credential whose scopes are a subset of, and whose lifetime does not exceed, those of the credential the hop received, with its audience limited to the next recipient. A sub-agent receives no broader tools, budget or autonomy level than its caller. The credential issuer or delegation policy, not the model, refuses delegation beyond a configured maximum chain depth or fan-out.
evidence: Delegation or token-exchange policy enforcing subset scopes, single audience and non-increasing lifetime per hop; test in which a sub-agent requesting broader scopes or tools is refused; test in which a chain one hop beyond the configured depth is refused
guidance: RFC 8693 treats nested actor claims as informational only for access decisions, so attenuation needs a fresh, narrowed token at each hop rather than a forwarded one. CoSAI Agentic IAM v1.0 (Mar 2026) says scope must not expand across hops and recommends a maximum delegation depth. Suggested defaults: depth 3, fan-out 10. Agent-to-agent authentication is BAL-6.21. Per-task runtime limits within one agent are BAL-6.12.

requirement: Access tokens used by the agent are bound to a key held by the agent runtime, and resource servers reject a token presented without proof of possession of that key, so a copied token cannot be replayed from elsewhere. The agent workload receives credentials only after presenting an attested workload identity that the issuer verifies.
evidence: Inventory of all access tokens and resource servers used by the asset, with coverage of key binding and workload attestation; token samples showing a key-confirmation claim or certificate binding; tests showing each resource server rejects captured tokens replayed without the key; issuer logs showing verified workload attestation before credential issuance.
guidance: For example DPoP (RFC 9449) or certificate-bound tokens over mutual TLS (RFC 8705), with attested workload identity such as SPIFFE or the IETF WIMSE work. Keep the key non-exportable and outside model-directed execution (BAL-2.11). Binding stops off-host replay, not misuse inside a compromised runtime. If any action class operates at A4, all access tokens used by that asset must meet BAL-2.13. An unsupported connection must be fixed or removed before A4 operation is allowed. The A4 conditions cannot be tailored or risk-accepted.

requirement: Each agent's initiation mode and its autonomy level (A0-A4) for each action class are recorded, and levels are enforced by permissions, approval settings and tool policy outside the model. Raising an action class, or deploying an agent with any class above A2, requires a promotion gate record showing: the target level's controls, as set by the re-assessed risk rating (BAL-1.5), implemented and tested; an operating record at a lower level for a defined minimum period; and owner and security sign-off (BAL-1.2). Agent identities cannot change their own level, tools, scopes or approval settings, or create agents, triggers or schedules at a higher level than their own. A4 requires a time-bound authorization recorded under BAL-1.13 of at most 6 months, renewed only through a new promotion gate record, approved by an executive risk owner, all applicable T2 and T3 controls and a tested kill switch (BAL-3.7), and is excluded where the asset reaches restricted or regulated data, makes or materially supports consequential decisions about individuals, takes irreversible financial actions, or fails BAL-3.5.
evidence: Asset register entries showing initiation mode and autonomy level per action class; promotion gate records with test results, operating-record data and owner and security sign-off, and any approved A3 actions, targets, limits and expiry; A4 authorization reference linked to its approved action classes and gate record; configuration showing the agent identity cannot modify its own tools, scopes or approval settings or create higher-level agents or schedules.
guidance: Action classes come from BAL-3.3 and BAL-3.6; the highest level feeds BAL-1.5. Suggested default: at least 30 days at the lower level, with action volume, approval rejections and edits, and incidents attached; for a new agent, a production pilot at A2 qualifies. Demotion needs no gate. Narrowing sub-agents' tools, scopes and budget is BAL-2.12. Prior art: Agentic Trust Framework (J. Woodruff, CSA blog, Feb 2026).

requirement: Every tool call an agent makes passes a policy enforcement point outside the model that: allows only tools on an allowlist keyed by the authenticated server or provider identity, the tool name and, for MCP servers, the tool-definition fingerprint approved under BAL-5.17; validates arguments against the tool's schema; enforces organization-defined argument constraints for the BAL-3.3 classes that carry BAL-3.6 high-risk actions, such as permitted recipients, destinations, paths and amounts; and records each decision in the agent action log (BAL-7.1). Calls that fail any check are denied.
evidence: Enforcement-point allowlist keyed by server identity, tool name and definition fingerprint; test results showing denial of an unlisted tool, a same-named tool from another server and an out-of-constraint recipient; sample decision records in the action log.
guidance: Tool names are unique only within one MCP server, and the MCP specification treats annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted, so key the allowlist on server identity. The enforcement point can be agent-framework middleware, an MCP gateway or proxy, or platform policy hooks (see the OWASP Agent Control Standard). Example constraints: external recipients limited to approved domains, writes limited to the task workspace, per-transaction amount caps. BAL-6.18 adds non-bypassability.

requirement: The organization assigns every tool, skill, plugin, connector and browser or computer-use action available to an agent to one or more capability classes, covering at least filesystem write, network egress, credential access, code execution, destructive, financial, identity or permission change, publishing and external communication; server-declared annotations and descriptions are not used as the classification. Policy is set per class, tools with no assigned class are denied, and MCP server-initiated sampling requests are disabled unless approved for that server.
evidence: Tool classification register listing each tool, its classes, who classified it and when; per-class policy configuration; test results showing that an unclassified tool and an MCP sampling request are rejected.
guidance: Classify by what a tool can do, not by its name or description; one tool can hold several classes. Adding a sensitive-data-read class lets the BAL-3.5 profile be derived from the classification. Re-classify when BAL-5.17 detects a definition change. MCP sampling lets a server request completions from the client's model, which gives the server a path to inject instructions.

requirement: Each token or grant an agent uses is issued for a single audience and carries only the scopes that a recorded mapping ties to the tools the agent is approved to use. Wildcard and administrative scopes, including organization-wide application permissions, require an approved exception (BAL-1.13). Every scope elevation or new consent for an agent identity is logged.
evidence: Scope-to-tool mapping for each agent; token and grant inventory showing audience and scopes per agent identity; approved exceptions for wildcard or administrative scopes and log entries for recent scope elevations.
guidance: Bind tokens to one resource, for example with OAuth resource indicators (RFC 8707), which the MCP authorization specification uses. Prefer fine-grained, per-resource tokens to broad personal access tokens: in the May 2025 GitHub MCP case, a token covering all of a user's repositories let an injected public issue expose private ones. Organization-wide application permissions (all mailboxes, all sites) count as wildcard scopes.

requirement: No assistant or agent session combines all three of: (A) content an attacker can influence, whether written inside or outside the organization, including email, web pages, shared documents, tickets, tool or MCP output and other agents' messages; (B) access to sensitive data or systems; and (C) any channel that changes state or leaves the trust boundary, including tool writes, outbound messages, URL fetches, rendered links or images, memory writes and networked code execution. A session may hold all three only if each (C) action is limited by a deterministic allowlist of recipients, destinations, parameters or render targets that the model cannot alter, individually approved under BAL-3.6, or removed by splitting the workflow so the part exposed to (A) holds no (B) or no (C). The A/B/C profile is recorded with the risk rating (BAL-1.5), reassessed when tools, connectors or sources change, and verified before release by testing (BAL-5.4) where the organization builds the asset, and otherwise by configuration review.
evidence: A/B/C profile recorded with the asset's risk rating; design record showing, for each (C) action in a session holding all three, the allowlist, approval or split applied; indirect-injection test results, or vendor configuration review, for the asset.
guidance: Named after Meta's Agents Rule of Two (Oct 2025), which builds on Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (Jun 2025); see ATLAS AML.M0030. Security operations, IT helpdesk and identity agents are A+B+C by default, because alerts, tickets and chats are attacker-authored. An asset holding all three is rated High (BAL-1.5), which brings in vendor evidence under BAL-8.6. Delimiting or detecting injected text does not break the combination.

requirement: A person authorized for the action class approves each action in these classes: payments and financial commitments; data transfer outside the trust boundary or to recipients not already entitled; secret retrieval or privileged credential use; external communications; destructive or irreversible operations, which in production also require a verified restore point; production changes, including protected-branch merges, releases and deployments; permission, access, credential or account-recovery changes; changes to security controls or monitoring, including closing or suppressing alerts; installing unapproved dependencies, extensions or MCP servers; and publishing to shared, public or personal destinations. The enforcement point, not the model, shows the exact action and full parameters with hidden or confusable characters revealed. Per-action approvals are single-use, bound to those parameters, and rejected when given by the acting agent's identity or, for merges, by the invoking user. At A3, an authorized person may approve specified actions and targets within recorded limits and an expiry date at the promotion gate (BAL-3.1). The system enforces those limits outside the model and blocks actions beyond them or after expiry. The agent cannot approve itself, and other required human reviews still apply.
evidence: Approval policy listing high-risk action classes and authorized approvers; approval prompts showing full parameters with hidden characters revealed; tests rejecting reused, altered and self-issued per-action approvals. Where A3 actions are pre-authorized, the promotion gate records approved actions, targets, limits and expiry, with tests showing actions outside the limits or after expiry are blocked and other required reviews remain enforced.
guidance: A model-written summary may accompany the parameters but never replaces them. Binding approvals to a hash of the parameters voids them on any change. A dependency already in the lockfile and resolved through the governed registry (BAL-5.20) counts as approved. Example A3 pre-authorization: refunds only to specified recipients, within per-refund and daily limits, until a set date. BAL-3.2 enforces those limits outside the model; BAL-3.13 protects the approval and any changes or renewals. Independent review of agent-authored merges under BAL-5.22 still applies. Motivating cases: Replit database deletion (Jul 2025), PixelLeak (Sep 2026).

requirement: An authorized operator can halt a single agent or a class of agents within a defined time objective. The halt revokes the agent's credentials and delegated grants (BAL-2.4), terminates its sessions and sandboxes, cancels its queued, scheduled and long-running tasks, disables triggers and webhooks it owns, reaches its sub-agents, and leaves in-flight transactions in a defined safe state; the triggers, schedules and sub-agents each agent creates are recorded so the halt can reach them. For vendor-operated agents the halt uses the vendor's admin controls, with contractual commitments covering any step those controls cannot perform. The halt is tested at least annually and after material change.
evidence: Kill-switch runbook naming authorized operators and the time objective; latest test record showing elapsed time, revoked credentials, canceled scheduled tasks and halted sub-agents; per-agent record of created triggers, schedules and sub-agents.
guidance: Suggested time objective: 15 minutes from decision to full effect. Access tokens that cannot be revoked need lifetimes shorter than the objective (BAL-2.4). Define safe states per transaction type, for example roll back, complete or hold for review. Test on a representative agent with a scheduled task and a sub-agent. Automatic tripping is BAL-3.11.

control: AI spend ceilings and usage anomaly alerting
requirement: Every model provider account, project and API key, and every self-hosted inference endpoint (BAL-1.8), has a usage or spend ceiling enforced by the provider or a gateway. Alerts fire at defined thresholds and on anomalous use, such as a new source identity, network, region or model, or a sudden burst. A documented runbook revokes the key or blocks the identity within a defined time.
evidence: Ceiling settings for each provider account, project, key and inference endpoint, reconciled to the BAL-1.8 inventory; alert rules and a recent alert with its handling; record of a timed key-revocation exercise.
guidance: LLMjacking uses stolen keys or cloud credentials to run models at the victim's expense; Unit 42 (Sep 2026) reported a victim's own AI endpoints turned into attack infrastructure. Disable model access in cloud accounts and regions with no approved use. Set ceilings with headroom and an override path; automatic suspension is optional, to avoid self-inflicted denial of service on customer-facing endpoints.

requirement: Rate limits and quotas are enforced per agent identity on model, tool and retrieval calls, and per external consumer (user, API key or tenant) of any AI endpoint exposed outside the organization. Systematic or high-volume querying of exposed endpoints that indicates model extraction, scraping or cost harvesting is detected.
evidence: Rate-limit and quota configuration per agent identity and per external consumer; detection rule for extraction or scraping patterns; record of a triggered limit or alert and how it was handled.
guidance: Combine short-term rate, burst and concurrency limits with longer-term quotas (ATLAS AML.M0004). Extraction and scraping signals include many near-duplicate queries, systematic coverage of an input space, unusual volume per key, and traffic spread across accounts to stay under limits. Per-agent limits work independently of budgets (BAL-3.10) and the kill switch.

requirement: Each agent and each workflow has defined caps on tokens, inference spend and external API spend. Alerts fire at defined fractions of each cap, and the agent or workflow is suspended automatically when a cap is reached until an authorized person resets or raises it.
evidence: Budget configuration per agent and workflow showing caps and alert thresholds; log of a budget alert and an automatic suspension; approval record for a cap reset or increase.
guidance: Apply caps across the whole workflow, because one request can start many model calls and tool actions (ATLAS AML.M0036). Suggested alert thresholds: 50% and 80% of each cap. Program-level ceilings in BAL-3.8 protect the provider account; these budgets contain a single runaway agent or workflow.

requirement: An agent is halted automatically, through the BAL-3.7 halt mechanism, when defined thresholds for execution limits (BAL-6.12) or activity anomalies (BAL-7.5) are crossed. The owner is alerted, and the agent resumes only when an authorized person releases it. Automatic tripping is tested at least quarterly.
evidence: Circuit-breaker rules linking each threshold to the halt mechanism; quarterly trip-test records showing time to halt; alert and release records for an actual or test trip.
guidance: Example trip conditions: an execution limit reached repeatedly within a window, a burst of destructive or egress actions, or an anomaly score above threshold. Test by injecting a synthetic threshold breach and confirming the halt completes within the BAL-3.7 time objective. Tripping uses the same halt as the manual kill switch, so test results for one support the other.

requirement: For each high-risk action class under BAL-3.6, approval rate, volume and time-to-decide are measured per approver at a defined cadence. Results that cross defined rubber-stamp thresholds trigger a recorded response: review of the approver and the class, fewer approval prompts through sandboxing or deterministic policy, or reassignment of the class.
evidence: Approval metrics per approver and action class for the last period; documented rubber-stamp thresholds; records of reviews, policy changes or reassignments those thresholds triggered.
guidance: Rubber-stamp signals: approval rates near 100% over meaningful volume, median decision times of a few seconds, or one approver handling a large share of a class. Anthropic reported that users approve 93% of Claude Code permission prompts (Mar 2026). Cutting prompt volume through sandboxing or deterministic policy often improves safety more than adding prompts. Addresses OWASP Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations T10, Overwhelming the Human in the Loop.

requirement: For the financial, permission-grant and irreversible production action classes of BAL-3.6, approval uses a separately authenticated channel that the agent cannot read or write. It shows either the individual transaction or the approved A3 actions, targets, limits and expiry. Changes or renewals need fresh approval through the same channel.
evidence: Configuration listing action classes using the separate approval channel; sample approvals showing transaction details or the approved A3 actions, targets, limits and expiry; access tests showing the agent cannot read or write the channel; tests rejecting expired or out-of-limit actions and changes or renewals without fresh approval.
guidance: Example: OpenID Connect CIBA with rich authorization requests (RFC 9396), deployed following RFC 10027 (BCP 247) on cross-device flows. The channel can be an authenticator push or a separate payments approval system, but not the chat, IDE or ticket session the agent operates in. Phishing-resistant authentication for approvers is recommended. An asset with none of these classes meets the control by recording that fact.

requirement: For each AI asset, handling rules are defined for every sensitivity label and data class the asset can reach. The rules state whether such content may be indexed or used to ground responses, stored in memory, submitted in prompts and returned in outputs, and the asset or its platform enforces them. Enforcement is verified with labeled test content at a defined interval and after vendor, model or configuration changes. If no labeling or classification scheme exists, or the asset cannot apply one, the control is not met; it is not recorded as not applicable.
evidence: Handling matrix for each asset mapping every label and data class to grounding, memory, prompt and output rules; latest labeled-content test results with date and trigger; change ticket showing re-verification after a vendor or configuration change.
guidance: From January 2026 a code defect (CW1226324) let Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat summarize Sent Items and Drafts labeled confidential despite DLP policy, so test vendor enforcement rather than assume it. Suggested defaults: test quarterly, and within 30 days of a relevant vendor change notice (BAL-8.8). For vendor assistants the rules are usually tenant settings, such as excluding labeled content from grounding.

requirement: Sensitivity labels and data classes on source content propagate to every artifact derived from it, including chunks, embeddings, summaries, memory entries and generated files, and retrieval and output handling apply the propagated label as they would the source label. Label changes at the source reach derived artifacts within a defined time. Where a store cannot carry labels, data classes that the BAL-4.1 handling rules do not approve for that store are not written to it.
evidence: Sample of chunks, embeddings and memory entries whose label metadata matches their sources; test showing a relabeled source reflected in retrieval within the defined time; list of stores that cannot carry labels, with the data classes excluded from each.
guidance: Suggested rule: an artifact derived from several sources takes the most restrictive source label. Suggested default relabel lag: 24 hours. This is T2 because label-aware chunking and vector metadata take engineering effort and vendor support is uneven; BAL-4.1 and BAL-4.7 provide the T1 baseline.

requirement: For each response, the identifiers and versions (or retrieval timestamps) of content that entered the model context, including retrieved documents or chunks, connector and tool results, and memory entries, are recorded with the interaction and retained under BAL-4.4. Records can be queried by response and by source, so that every response that used a given source within a period can be identified.
evidence: Interaction record for a sampled response listing source and chunk identifiers with versions; query output listing all responses in a period that used a named source; retention setting for lineage records.
guidance: Querying by source is what makes incident scoping possible once a poisoned, overshared or mislabeled source is found (BAL-7.4). Full reconstruction of an alert is BAL-7.9. Record identifiers rather than copies of content, so lineage does not become another sensitive store. Lineage of model training data is BAL-4.13 and BAL-5.15.

requirement: Retention periods are defined per data class for every store of AI content the asset creates or uses, and are enforced by deletion or by vendor retention settings. The stores include prompts and responses, content held in logs, memory, embeddings and retrieval indexes, caches, intermediate artifacts and vendor-held copies. Legal hold and records obligations, including the minimum retention of agent action records (BAL-7.1), override scheduled deletion and limit deletion requests as applicable law allows. Deletion requests, including data-subject requests, reach every one of these stores within the applicable deadline.
evidence: Retention schedule listing each AI store, including memory and vendor-held copies, with the period per data class and the enforcement method; vendor retention or zero-retention settings in use; record of one data-subject deletion traced through all AI stores.
guidance: Some vendor stores sit outside platform retention tooling: Microsoft documents that Purview retention does not apply to Microsoft 365 Copilot memory. Record such stores and their deletion path, or turn them off (BAL-4.10). Deleting a source should also delete its chunks and embeddings (BAL-4.9). Agent action records keep the BAL-7.1 minimum. Where personal data tunes a model, the DPIA (BAL-1.12) records how erasure requests are honored.

requirement: Data loss prevention inspects AI channels wherever technically possible. These include browser, desktop and mobile AI apps, IDE and CLI tools, model APIs, SaaS-embedded assistants, agent tool-call arguments, and agent writes to email, tickets and repositories. A coverage map records, for each AI channel in use, whether it is inspected and what is enforced. Each uninspected channel has a documented compensating control or an exception under BAL-1.13.
evidence: AI channel coverage map with inspection status, enforced policies and review date; DLP policy configuration covering AI destinations and agent tool calls; compensating-control or exception record for each uninspected channel.
guidance: Agent writes are a common blind spot: an agent that posts a summary to a ticket or pushes to a repository is using an egress channel (AML.T0086). Use the same data class definitions as BAL-4.1 and BAL-4.6. Suggested default: review the map at least annually and whenever a new AI channel is approved (BAL-1.6). Use of unsanctioned AI services is handled under BAL-8.9.

requirement: Before content that the organization or its users send reaches a model, a third-party API, a retrieval index or agent memory, data classes that destination is not approved to receive are blocked or redacted. Approval for model providers and third-party services comes from their BAL-8.7 profile, and for indexes and memory from the asset's BAL-4.1 handling rules. Secrets and credentials are removed whatever the destination, using detection that covers the credential formats the organization uses.
evidence: Matrix of destinations and approved data classes, traced to BAL-8.7 profiles and BAL-4.1 rules; block or redaction configuration at the client, gateway or ingestion pipeline; test results showing seeded restricted data and sample credentials stopped before each destination type.
guidance: Destination-aware means claim data can go to a model contracted for it while the same data is blocked from an unapproved model; blanket redaction breaks approved use. Indexes and memory are destinations because credentials stored there can later be retrieved by an agent (AML.T0082). Content a vendor assistant retrieves for itself is governed by BAL-4.1 grounding rules and BAL-4.8, not by this control.

requirement: At query time, retrieval checks each item against the requesting principal's entitlements and removes unauthorized items before they reach the model. For an agent acting for a user, the principal is that user within the limits of BAL-2.3; only an agent with no requesting user, such as an event-triggered agent, uses its own identity's entitlements (BAL-2.1). Checks use access-control metadata propagated from the source or a late-binding check against it, and source permission changes take effect within a defined time. Response and semantic caches serve content only to requesters entitled to its sources.
evidence: Retrieval design showing where entitlement filtering occurs and which metadata or source check it uses; test in which users with different permissions run the same query and receive only entitled items, plus a revocation test against the defined time; cache key configuration showing entitlement scope.
guidance: Apply the entitlement filter inside the similarity query or re-check every item passed to the model; loose namespace or tenant filters are a known cause of cross-tenant leakage (LLM09:2026). Suggested default permission-change lag: 1 hour. Key caches by entitlement scope, or disable them for restricted classes. Provider-side prompt-cache isolation is evidenced under BAL-8.3. Permission hygiene in the sources themselves is BAL-4.8.

requirement: Before a retrieval-grounded assistant or agent is enabled for a population, and at a defined interval afterward, the content it can ground on for that population is assessed for oversharing, covering organization-wide or anonymous links, all-employee groups, stale or inherited access, and content without an active owner. Each overshared or highly sensitive finding is remediated, excluded from grounding as a time-bound interim measure with a named owner, or accepted under BAL-1.13. Enablement for a new population waits until all its findings are dispositioned.
evidence: Oversharing assessment for each enabled population with findings and dispositions; register of interim grounding exclusions with owner and end date; enablement approval for the latest population that references its completed assessment.
guidance: Copilots that ground through users' permissions surface whatever those users can already open, which turns permission debt into search results. Microsoft's Copilot deployment blueprint puts oversharing remediation first, and its Restricted Content Discovery is an example of a temporary exclusion that leaves permissions unchanged. Suggested defaults: reassess at least every 6 months; interim exclusions last 6 months or less. Query-time enforcement for built retrieval is BAL-4.7.

control: RAG source registration and trust labeling
requirement: Each source indexed for retrieval is registered with an owner, the population that can write to it, and an origin class: curated internal, user-generated internal, or external or inbound. Chunks from external or inbound sources, and from any source writable beyond its approved writer set, are marked untrusted, and an asset that retrieves them carries the UNTRUSTED tag, so that BAL-3.5, BAL-6.2 and BAL-6.3 apply to them. Indexed content is traceable to its source and removable by source. For vendor-managed indexes, the externally writable sources are recorded and accepted by the asset owner.
evidence: Source register with owner, writer population and origin class for each indexed source; sample retrieved chunks carrying the untrusted marker and origin metadata; record of removing all chunks of a test source by its identifier.
guidance: Retrieval permissions (BAL-4.7) do not help when an attacker's content is legitimately readable. GeminiJack (disclosed December 2025) used a shared document, invite or email retrieved during enterprise search. PoisonedRAG (USENIX Security 2025) reached about 90% attack success with five injected texts per target question. For assistants the organization does not build, record externally writable sources as condition (A) of the BAL-3.5 profile. Origin classes are defined below.

requirement: Persistent memory (saved memories, conversation summaries and agent-managed state) is enabled for an asset only when all of the following hold, and is otherwise turned off: (a) memory is scoped to the user, tenant and agent it belongs to (and to the session, for session-bound state), and any memory shared beyond that scope is explicitly approved; (b) each write records its source and is logged; (c) writes triggered by content the user did not author, including retrieved documents, tool output and prompts prefilled through links, are blocked or require explicit user confirmation; (d) users and administrators can view and delete entries individually and by source; (e) retention follows BAL-4.4, and data classes the BAL-4.1 handling rules do not approve for memory are not stored.
evidence: Memory settings for each asset showing enabled state, scope and shared-memory approvals; sample write log with source attribution; test results showing a write proposed by a retrieved document or prefilled link blocked or held for confirmation, and entries deleted by source.
guidance: Microsoft reported in February 2026 more than 50 prefilled-prompt 'Summarize with AI' links from 31 companies that planted memories favoring a source (AML.T0130, AML.T0131). Microsoft documents that Microsoft 365 Copilot memory lacks Purview retention, audit logging and admin control over writes; where a vendor offers no such controls, memory stays off. Memory status is inventoried in BAL-1.10. Detection of risky writes is BAL-7.12, where implemented.

requirement: Before model output is returned to a user or passed to a downstream system, it is checked for secrets and credentials using detection that covers the credential formats the organization uses, and any found are removed whatever the recipient. Other sensitive data classes in output are released only to recipients and destinations authorized for those classes.
evidence: Output inspection configuration listing the credential formats and data classes covered; test results showing seeded credentials removed and a restricted data class withheld from an unauthorized recipient; sample logged redaction events.
guidance: Recipient-aware release lets an HR partner receive an employee's record while an agent emailing outside the organization cannot include it. Credentials reach output through retrieval (AML.T0082), tool results and memory, so input checks (BAL-4.6) do not replace this one. Exfiltration through rendered links and images is BAL-6.3. Measured guardrail efficacy is BAL-5.11, where implemented.

requirement: Citations in retrieval-grounded output are generated by the retrieval layer from identifiers of items the requester was authorized to retrieve under BAL-4.7, not composed by the model. A citation can therefore point only to an item actually retrieved for that response. Each citation shows the source location and the source's origin class from BAL-4.9.
evidence: Design showing citations assembled from retrieval identifiers; test in which the model is induced to cite a fabricated or non-retrieved source and no such citation is shown; sample citation displaying location and origin class.
guidance: Citations make an answer look authoritative, and crafted or poisoned content exploits that (AML.T0067.000). Showing the origin class tells readers whether an answer rests on a curated policy or on inbound email. For decision-support uses, withholding or flagging uncited answers is optional. Groundedness scoring is BAL-6.9. Neither citations nor groundedness shows that sources are free of poisoning.

requirement: Data used to train, fine-tune or evaluate models the organization builds or adapts has its sources and content hashes recorded, and the hashes are verified when the data is used. Write access to training and evaluation datasets and to training pipelines is restricted to authorized identities and logged, and changes are reviewed before use. Each resulting model passes regression testing (BAL-5.5) and the adversarial security test suite (BAL-5.3) before release.
evidence: Dataset manifest with sources, versions and content hashes for a recent training or fine-tuning run; access list and change log for training data stores and pipelines, with review approvals; release record with BAL-5.5 and BAL-5.3 results.
guidance: Do not rely on poisoning detection alone. Track what enters training data and who can change it. Souly et al. (2025) demonstrated a narrow gibberish-output backdoor in models from 600M to 13B parameters using about 250 poisoned documents; this result concerns the models and attack tested. Evaluation sets are in scope because a tampered set hides regressions. Model lineage and signing are BAL-5.15.

requirement: The following are versioned so that each can be restored to a known-good state after poisoning or compromise: model versions (or, for provider-hosted models, the pinned model reference), system prompts and templates, retrieval indexes with snapshots of their sources, agent memory stores, and agent configurations. Restoration of each is tested at least annually.
evidence: Version history for the prompts, configurations, indexes and memory of a sampled asset; most recent restore test with scope, duration and result; restore steps referenced from the BAL-7.4 playbook for poisoned indexes or memory.
guidance: Keep restore points long enough to predate likely poisoning dwell time; suggested default is 90 days for indexes and memory. For provider-hosted models, restoration means re-pinning a prior snapshot while the provider still offers it (BAL-5.2); otherwise use the BAL-8.13 fallback. AML.M0031 includes rollback of poisoned memory as part of memory hardening.

requirement: Model weights, adapters and fine-tuned checkpoints are classified at least as high as the most sensitive data used to train or tune them. They are stored, accessed, exported and deleted under that classification's controls. Inference access to a fine-tuned or customized model, including one hosted by a vendor, is limited to principals entitled to the data used to tune it.
evidence: Classification records for weights, adapters and checkpoints showing the highest training-data class; access and export logs for model storage or registry; inference access policy for each tuned model compared with the entitlement group for its tuning data.
guidance: A model tuned on claims or HR data and opened to all employees bypasses retrieval permissions, because training records can be inferred or extracted through queries (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001). Where wider access is needed, record a BAL-1.13 exception supported by memorization and extraction testing. Weight file integrity and signing are BAL-5.14 and BAL-5.15.

requirement: Retrieval frequency is tracked for each indexed item. Items retrieved for an anomalously broad range of unrelated queries (adversarial hubs), or showing other defined signs of embedding-space manipulation, are flagged against defined thresholds. Flagged items are reviewed and, if found adversarial, quarantined from retrieval.
evidence: Retrieval frequency report for each item, with thresholds; review and quarantine record for a flagged item; test showing a seeded hub item is flagged.
guidance: Hub-based retrieval attacks and their defences are still research topics and tooling is immature, hence T3. The same per-item telemetry can also reveal near-duplicate flooding of an index. Quarantine relies on removal by source (BAL-4.9) and, where implemented, restoration (BAL-4.14).

requirement: Before production, each AI application or agent in scope has a documented threat model that identifies its trust boundaries, every untrusted input path, every high-impact sink (tool actions, data egress including rendered links and images, code execution and external communication) and its delegation chains. For each path from an untrusted source to a high-impact sink, the threat model records the control that constrains the path and the test or gate (BAL-5.3, BAL-5.4 or BAL-5.6) that verifies it. It is updated at each autonomy promotion (BAL-3.1) and each material change under BAL-5.2.
evidence: Threat model for a sampled asset with data-flow diagram, untrusted inputs, high-impact sinks and delegation chains; source-to-sink table naming the control and test for each path; revision history showing an update at the last autonomy promotion or material change.
guidance: A data-flow diagram plus a source-to-sink table is enough. The BAL-3.5 capability profile is a useful starting point. ETSI EN 304 223 requires threat analysis (provision 5.1.3-1) and requires it to be repeated when settings or configuration change (5.1.3-1.1). ATLAS techniques and the OWASP Top 10 lists work as threat checklists. Treat rendered links and images as sinks, because they can carry data out (BAL-6.3).

requirement: Changes to an AI asset's model (version or snapshot, fine-tunes, adapters, merges, quantized variants, and provider-initiated updates, alias re-pointing and retirements), system prompts and templates, tools and MCP servers, retrieval sources, guardrail and agent-policy configuration, and autonomy levels are recorded in a history the person making the change cannot alter, impact-assessed, approved by someone other than the author (BAL-1.2), and pass BAL-5.5 and the BAL-5.6 release gate before reaching production. Model references pin a specific version or snapshot where the provider offers one; where it does not, a provider-initiated change is re-tested within a defined period of its notice or detection. The AI bill of materials (BAL-1.7) is updated with each change.
evidence: Change records for the last three changes showing author, independent approver, impact assessment and linked test results; configuration showing pinned model versions or snapshots; AI bill of materials entry updated with the last model or tool change.
guidance: Treat provider notices of model updates, alias changes and retirements (BAL-8.8) as changes, and prefer dated snapshot IDs to aliases such as 'latest'. Suggested re-test period for unpinnable provider changes: 5 business days. Policy as code and automatic AI-BOM regeneration at each release are implementation options. Narrow fine-tuning can broadly degrade safety (Betley et al., Nature 2026), so treat fine-tunes and adapters like any other change.

requirement: Each AI asset the organization builds or configures has a maintained adversarial test suite, reviewed and updated at a defined interval, that is run before every release under BAL-5.6. The suite covers direct prompt injection, jailbreaks and disclosure of sensitive data or hidden context for every asset; tool misuse and excessive-agency cases for assets that call tools; and, for assets rated High or Critical, organization-specific scenarios derived from the threat model (BAL-5.1) or, where none is required, from the factors that drove the rating.
evidence: Test suite inventory listing attack families and case counts for a sampled asset; the last two run reports with pass and fail results; record of the last suite review, including organization-specific scenarios for a sampled High or Critical asset.
guidance: Public test catalogs such as the OWASP AI Testing Guide and benchmarks such as AgentDojo and JailbreakBench are a starting point. Organization-specific cases use the asset's real tools, data classes and personas. Suggested review interval: every six months, and when a new attack class is published. Static suites overstate robustness. Adaptive testing is BAL-5.9 (T2).

requirement: Before release, indirect prompt injection is tested on every untrusted input path identified in the threat model (BAL-5.1), such as retrieved documents, tool and MCP output, fetched web content, email, text extracted from images or files, and messages from other agents. On each path, tests attempt to exfiltrate planted canary data through tool calls and through rendered links and images, and confirm that the capability separation recorded under BAL-3.5 holds.
evidence: Coverage matrix mapping each untrusted input path in the threat model to test cases; run report showing canary exfiltration attempts per path and their outcomes; test evidence that a session holding untrusted content could not trigger an unapproved external action.
guidance: Plant unique canary strings in data the asset can reach and watch for them at controlled endpoints. Include hidden text (white-on-white, Unicode tag characters, metadata, text in images) and instructions that trigger on a later turn. EchoLeak (Jun 2025, email) and ForcedLeak (Sep 2025, web form) show the pattern: outside content is retrieved as context, then data leaves through a rendered or fetched URL.

requirement: A maintained baseline set of security and safety scenarios with expected outcomes, including a case for each security defect found through testing, incidents or external reports (BAL-7.4), is re-run on every change in scope of BAL-5.2, including fine-tunes, adapters, model merges and quantized variants. A regression beyond a defined tolerance blocks the release.
evidence: Baseline scenario set with expected outcomes and change history, including cases added from defects; test logs showing the set ran for the last model and prompt change; the defined tolerance and any release blocked by a regression.
guidance: Keep the baseline separate from the adversarial suite so results stay comparable across versions. Suggested tolerance: no new failure in any security-critical case, and an aggregate drop of no more than about 2 percentage points. Valid reports received through the BAL-7.4 external reporting channel become regression cases once fixed.

requirement: A release gate blocks production release of a new asset, or of a change under BAL-5.2, unless: (a) where BAL-5.1 applies, the threat model shows no path from an untrusted source to a high-impact sink without BAL-3.6 approval or an equivalent deterministic control; (b) BAL-5.3, BAL-5.4 and BAL-5.5 results for the categories applicable to the asset, including sensitive-data disclosure, are within defined thresholds; (c) every canary exfiltration attempt under BAL-5.4 fails; and (d) for assets rated High or Critical, the role named under BAL-1.2 approves the release. The gate runs in the build pipeline where one exists; for low-code agents it is a documented pre-publish test sign-off.
evidence: Gate checklist or pipeline configuration with criteria and thresholds; release record for a sampled asset linking threat model, test results and approver; a release the gate blocked, or the pre-publish sign-off for a low-code agent.
guidance: Set thresholds per category: for example, zero failures for canary exfiltration and for tool-misuse cases that reach a high-impact sink, and a defined maximum attack success rate for each jailbreak family. Where BAL-5.9 is implemented, its threshold also blocks release. Results go to the AI governance owner under BAL-1.12. Exceptions follow BAL-1.13.
