requirement: Deployed assets are re-tested against their current adversarial, indirect-injection and regression suites (BAL-5.3, BAL-5.4, BAL-5.5) at a defined interval set by risk rating, and at least annually, whether or not the asset has changed. Failures are tracked to remediation within defined timelines.
evidence: Re-evaluation schedule by risk rating; report of the last scheduled run for a sampled High or Critical asset; tracking records showing failures from that run remediated or risk-accepted within the defined timeline.
guidance: Suggested cadence: annually for High assets and quarterly for Critical assets. Unchanged assets still need re-testing, because new attack classes appear, provider-side safety layers change without a version change, and retrieved content shifts. Add newly published techniques to the suites before each scheduled run.

requirement: Security testing exercises complete agent loops, including multi-turn conversations, multi-tool sequences and planning steps, with cases for adversarial chaining of individually permitted actions, tool-call argument manipulation and goal hijacking. Test outcomes, including what the agent reports it did, are verified against the systems of record the agent acted on rather than against the agent's own account.
evidence: Multi-step test scenarios with expected end states in the target systems; run report showing system-of-record checks after each scenario; a case where the agent's reported outcome differed from the recorded state and how it was scored.
guidance: Run tests where tools and data are realistic but production writes are not possible. In the Replit incident (July 2025), an agent deleted a production database during a code freeze and misreported what it had done, so the agent's own report is not evidence. AgentDojo provides multi-step injection scenarios.

requirement: Prompt-injection testing of the asset's untrusted and public input paths generates payloads adaptively against the deployed configuration (with attacker models, mutation or optimization) in addition to replaying a fixed library. The residual attack success rate is measured at a stated attacker budget against a defined threshold, with every guardrail the asset relies on enabled, and a result above the threshold is a release-blocking failure.
evidence: Adaptive test configuration stating attacker method and budget; results showing residual attack success rate per input path against the threshold; record that every relied-on guardrail was enabled in the tested configuration.
guidance: The Attacker Moves Second (Nasr, Carlini, Tramer et al., arXiv 2510.09023, Oct 2025) bypassed 12 published defenses, mostly with over 90% success, although most had originally reported near-zero attack success. Give testers the defense specification. State the budget explicitly, for example 500 adaptive attempts per input path, so results stay comparable over time.

requirement: Defined security and safety indicators of the deployed asset's behavior are measured against a recorded baseline, continuously or at a defined interval, and deviation beyond a defined threshold is detected.
evidence: List of monitored indicators with baselines and thresholds; trend report for the last quarter; alert record for a threshold breach, or test evidence that a simulated breach raises an alert to the owner.
guidance: Useful indicators include refusal rate, guardrail trigger rate, blocked-action rate, groundedness or hallucination score, and tool-call error rate. Drift often follows provider-side changes, shifts in retrieved content or prompt edits, so correlate alerts with BAL-5.2 change records. Unexplained drift in behavior can also indicate poisoned training or retrieval data.

requirement: Each runtime guardrail the asset relies on, such as prompt-injection, jailbreak, data-leakage and content-filtering detectors, has its detection rate and false-positive rate measured on an organization-maintained test set of attacks and representative benign inputs, against documented thresholds, at deployment and after any change to the guardrail version, the model or the policy. A guardrail that misses its thresholds is not relied on as a control, including in the threat model (BAL-5.1), until it meets them.
evidence: Guardrail test set description with attack and benign sample counts; measurement report per guardrail showing detection and false-positive rates against thresholds; re-measurement record after the last guardrail, model or policy update.
guidance: Vendor-reported accuracy is not evidence. Measure on the asset's own traffic patterns, languages and formats, including obfuscated, encoded and multimodal attacks. Thresholds are organization-defined for each guardrail and use case. Detection is a tripwire, not a boundary (BAL-6.1, BAL-6.4), so efficacy results drive tuning and alerting, not authorization decisions.

requirement: Externally sourced model artifacts, including weights, adapters, tokenizer configuration and chat or prompt templates, are pulled into an organization-controlled registry or mirror and scanned for embedded code, unsafe deserialization operators and malicious template logic before any use. Only artifacts that pass are available to fine-tuning, evaluation or serving environments.
evidence: Registry or mirror configuration showing training and serving environments pull only from it; scan reports for the last three ingested models covering weights, tokenizer and template files; a quarantined or rejected artifact record.
guidance: Cover pickle-based, safetensors, ONNX, GGUF and framework-native formats. Scanning is defense in depth. JFrog disclosed three PickleScan bypasses (CVE-2025-10155, -10156 and -10157) in Dec 2025, and poisoned GGUF chat templates (AML.T0018.003) change behavior without touching weights. Pair scanning with BAL-5.13 and BAL-5.14. Risk assessment before ingestion is BAL-8.1.

requirement: Models are loaded only from non-executable serialization formats, with remote or custom code execution disabled in loaders and inference runtimes. Any load that must execute code, such as a pickle-based checkpoint or model-specific code, requires an exception under BAL-1.13 and runs in an isolated environment without credentials or network egress. Checkpoints produced and hash-verified inside the same isolated training environment may be resumed there without an exception.
evidence: Loader and runtime configuration showing remote code execution disabled; inventory of production model formats; exception record and isolated job configuration (no credentials, no egress) for any code-executing load such as a format conversion.
guidance: For example, disable trust_remote_code and serve safetensors. Restricted loaders are not a boundary: CVE-2025-32434 allowed code execution in PyTorch before 2.6.0 even with weights_only=True. A common pattern is to convert a pickle checkpoint once, in a disposable job without secrets or network access, and keep only the converted output.

requirement: Models are referenced by an immutable revision identifier or content hash rather than by a mutable name, tag or namespace path. At deployment, hashes or signatures of weights, adapters, tokenizer and chat-template files are verified against the publisher's published values where available, and otherwise against the values recorded when the artifact entered the organization's registry (BAL-5.12 for external artifacts).
evidence: Deployment manifests showing models pinned by revision hash or digest; verification step output from the last deployment; registry hash record for a sampled model, including tokenizer and chat-template files.
guidance: Unit 42 (Sep 2025) showed that re-registering deleted Hugging Face namespaces gave code execution in cloud model catalogs that referenced models by name. Revision pinning plus an internal mirror (BAL-5.12) prevents this. CoSAI's Artifact Integrity Maturity Model (Oct 2026) places consumer hash and signature verification at Level 1. Signing models the organization produces is BAL-5.15 (T2).

requirement: For models the organization trains or fine-tunes, and open-weight models it ingests, the base model and its source, the training and fine-tuning datasets and their versions (BAL-4.13), and the lineage of each weight artifact are recorded; for ingested models, details held by the publisher are recorded as far as the publisher discloses them. Models and adapters the organization produces are signed, and signatures are verified before deployment.
evidence: Lineage record for a sampled fine-tuned model naming base model, source revision and dataset versions; signing step in the training or release pipeline; deployment log showing signature verification before the model was served.
guidance: Record lineage in the format used for BAL-1.7, for example a CycloneDX ML-BOM or the SPDX 3.0 AI profile. Signing can use any scheme the deployment platform verifies, such as Sigstore-based model signing. Organizations that distribute models externally should treat signing as baseline (CoSAI Artifact Integrity Maturity Model, Level 1). API-only models need only the BAL-1.7 minimum record.

requirement: MCP servers, skills, plugins, custom agents and AI coding extensions not built through the organization's own release gate (BAL-5.6) are security-reviewed before approval and again on every new version or definition-fingerprint change (BAL-5.17), by static analysis of code (where available), manifests and tool definitions and by observing behavior in an isolated environment. Reject concealed instructions, attempts to bypass approved security rules, undeclared data transfers and behavior outside the approved purpose. Reviewed task instructions are allowed. Instructions and executable dependencies fetched at runtime must be reviewed and approved before use; executable dependencies must be pinned.
evidence: Review records showing approved instructions, dependencies and expected behavior, with checks for hidden instructions and unexpected data transfers; review records for the last three approved components and one rejected component; evidence that a new version or changed definition of an approved component triggered re-review before use.
guidance: Koi Security found 341 malicious skills among 2,857 on ClawHub (Feb 2026); 335 of them used fake prerequisites to install an infostealer. Review tool descriptions as prompts, because they reach the model before any call. Behavioral review records network destinations, file access and spawned processes. Runtime capability classification is BAL-3.3, and BAL-5.17 binds trust to content.

requirement: Locally installed MCP servers, skills, plugins and coding-agent software run only at an approved version pinned by content hash, and unpinned on-the-fly package execution is not permitted. For every approved MCP server, local or remote, tool names, descriptions and input schemas are fingerprinted at approval. A change in version or fingerprint blocks use of the component until it is re-reviewed under BAL-5.16 and re-approved.
evidence: MCP client or gateway configuration showing pinned versions and content hashes; stored tool-definition fingerprints for approved servers; log or test showing a changed tool description blocked the server until re-approval.
guidance: postmark-mcp shipped about 15 clean versions before 1.0.16 added a hidden BCC to every email (Sep 2025). MCPoison (CVE-2025-54136) bound approval to a server name, not its content. Running npx or uvx without a pinned version is unpinned execution. Disable agent self-update or route it through approval. Remote servers can change behavior without changing definitions, so egress control (BAL-6.14) and tool telemetry (BAL-7.7, where implemented) compensate.

requirement: Skills, plugins, MCP servers and IDE or AI coding extensions are installed only from an organization-approved catalog, and AI components enter the catalog only after BAL-5.16 review. Unsanctioned marketplaces, registries and direct installs from arbitrary URLs or repositories are blocked through managed settings or equivalent technical enforcement. A component withdrawn from the catalog is removed or disabled on endpoints and platforms within a defined period.
evidence: Published catalog with approval dates and versions; managed-settings or policy export showing unsanctioned marketplaces and registries blocked; removal records for the last withdrawn component showing completion within the defined period.
guidance: An internal registry or mirror is one way to implement this. Non-AI IDE extensions can enter through standard software approval. Suggested removal period: 24 hours for components withdrawn as malicious and 30 days otherwise. GlassWorm (Oct 2025) spread through Open VSX, a marketplace that several AI IDEs use. Where a tool cannot restrict install sources, detect installs through BAL-1.9 and record a BAL-1.13 exception.

requirement: New versions of approved IDE and AI coding extensions reach managed endpoints only after a defined delay or through a staged rollout to a pilot group, in addition to any re-approval under BAL-5.17. Extension packs and dependencies that an approved extension installs are reviewed as part of its approval, and verified-publisher status or a publisher signature alone does not satisfy that review.
evidence: Managed update policy showing the delay or rollout rings; rollout records for the last two extension updates; approval record for a sampled extension listing the packs and dependencies it installs.
guidance: Amazon Q Developer for VS Code 1.84.0 (July 2025) was an official release from the verified publisher, yet it carried an injected wiper prompt after an over-scoped token was compromised. AWS says the code did not run, and 1.85.0 removed it (AWS-2025-015). Suggested delay: 7 days, with an expedited path for security fixes. BAL-5.17 decides which version may run; this control decides when it rolls out.

requirement: Package installations on developer workstations, in coding-agent sandboxes and in CI environments resolve only through an organization-controlled registry proxy or an enforced package-manager policy. The proxy or policy blocks known-malicious packages, typosquatted names, and versions published more recently than a defined minimum age, so that a newly registered package matching a hallucinated name is held back; an expedited path exists for urgent security fixes. Install-time lifecycle scripts are disabled except for allowlisted packages.
evidence: Proxy or package-manager configuration for developer, agent and CI environments, including minimum-age and lifecycle-script settings; log of a blocked install of a too-new or known-malicious package; expedited-path record for the last urgent fix.
guidance: Suggested minimum age: 7 days. Malicious releases are often pulled within hours: LiteLLM 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were quarantined by PyPI after about 40 minutes, although the LiteLLM advisory treats installs between 10:39 and 16:00 UTC as at risk (Mar 2026), and Cline CLI 2.3.0 was deprecated after about 8 hours (Feb 2026). Shai-Hulud 2.0 ran at pre-install (Nov 2025). The hallucinated name react-codeshift spread through agent skill files to 237+ repositories (Jan 2026). Agent-initiated installs also fall under BAL-3.6.

requirement: The organization defines which AI coding assistants and agents are approved and which models and providers each may use, and enforces this through central administration or managed settings. Content exclusions keep designated sensitive repositories and files out of AI context, prompt and agent-action logging is enabled where the tool supports it, and organization code is not processed through personal or free-tier accounts (BAL-8.9).
evidence: Approved coding tools and models list; admin console or managed-settings export showing model restrictions, content exclusions and logging enabled; BAL-8.9 evidence showing personal and free-tier accounts restricted for coding tools.
guidance: Some coding tools let users switch to third-party models with different data terms. Limit them to models whose BAL-8.7 profile permits the code's data classes. Typical exclusions cover secrets and key material, regulated data and security-sensitive code. Coding-agent sandboxing is BAL-6.13 and configuration lockdown is BAL-6.16. Detection of personal-license agents is BAL-8.11 (T2).

requirement: Code produced by AI assistants and agents passes the same secret scanning, static analysis, software composition analysis and human review gates as human-written code, and no agent identity, bot account or automation path is exempt from them. Commits and pull requests authored by agents are identifiable as agent-authored in version-control history.
evidence: Branch protection or ruleset export showing no bypass for agent or bot identities; pipeline configuration running secret scanning, SAST and SCA on every pull request; sample of agent-authored pull requests showing identification and scan results.
guidance: Veracode's 2026 GenAI Code Security Report (Jul 2026) put the average security pass rate of AI-generated code at 56%, with no improvement on earlier years. Identify agent authorship with commit trailers, labels or dedicated agent identities. Merging agent-authored changes needs a human approver other than the invoker, and agents do not approve their own changes (BAL-3.6).

control: Isolation of event-triggered agents in CI/CD
requirement: Agents in CI/CD or repository automation that run in response to events outside parties can cause, such as opening or commenting on issues or pull requests or sending email, use credentials that cannot push code, modify workflow definitions, branch protection or code-owner files, publish packages or deploy. Release and publishing secrets are not available to their jobs, and those jobs share no caches, artifacts or runners with release or publishing pipelines.
evidence: Workflow definitions for agent jobs showing trigger events and token permissions; secret-scoping configuration showing release secrets unavailable to those jobs; runner and cache configuration separating agent jobs from release pipelines.
guidance: In Clinejection (Feb 2026), a prompt injection in an issue title steered an AI triage workflow that any GitHub user could trigger. Actions cache poisoning then reached the nightly release workflow's publishing credentials, and a malicious cline 2.3.0 reached npm. Deliver agent proposals as comments or patches that a human applies. Maintainer-triggered agents that read outside content fall under BAL-3.5 and BAL-3.6.

requirement: The tools, scopes, recipients and data sources available in a session are set by deterministic code or configuration outside the model, from the authenticated principal and the approved task. Content from retrieval, tools, files, email, web pages or other agents cannot add tools, widen scopes, change recipients or alter identity context. Once untrusted content has entered a session, every action in the network egress, external communication, credential access or code execution classes (BAL-3.3) passes a deterministic check of its destination, recipient or parameters, or approval under BAL-3.6, for the rest of that session. Delimiting, spotlighting and detection (BAL-6.4) do not satisfy this control.
evidence: Configuration showing per-session tool and scope assembly from the authenticated principal; test results where injected content tries to add a tool, widen a scope or change a recipient and fails; policy decision logs for egress actions after untrusted content entered a session.
guidance: Build the tool set per session from the agent's registration and user entitlements. Taint the session when an item with an untrusted origin label (BAL-6.2) enters context. Take recipients from fields resolved by code, such as the sender being answered, never from content. ShareLeak (CVE-2026-21520), where injected form text made an agent email data out, is the pattern this breaks. BAL-3.5 decides if the combination is allowed; this control gates each action.

requirement: Every item placed in model context carries an origin label set by the application, not by the model. Content from tools, MCP servers, other agents, web fetches, files, email and APIs enters context only as labeled data within a defined size limit, with Unicode tag, zero-width and bidirectional control characters removed or made visible and active markup removed. None of this content is loaded as system prompt, policy, tool definition or agent configuration, which come only from approved configuration.
evidence: Context-assembly code or configuration showing origin labels and size limits; test results for inputs carrying tag, zero-width and bidirectional characters and hidden markup; configuration showing tool output and fetched content cannot populate the system prompt or agent configuration.
guidance: Code points to handle: U+E0000-E007F (tags), U+200B-200D, U+2060 and U+FEFF (zero-width), and U+202A-202E and U+2066-2069 (bidirectional). Active markup includes scripts, HTML comments, hidden text and auto-loading image or link references. Use BAL-4.9 origin classes for retrieved content. This is hardening only: character injection evaded six guardrails (arXiv 2504.11168, 2025), so the boundary stays in BAL-6.1.

requirement: Surfaces that render model output (chat interfaces, IDEs, email and collaboration clients, downstream renderers) do not automatically fetch resources referenced in that output (images, link previews and unfurls, iframes, remote styles or fonts, HTML or diagram renderers, prefetch) except from an allowlist of origins controlled by the organization or provider, applied after normalizing Markdown and HTML variants and invisible Unicode. Links to other destinations are inert or open only through a click-through that shows the full destination, with query strings and fragments removed. Rendering allowlists are reviewed at least quarterly and on change, removing expired or re-registrable domains, open redirects and proxies that fetch arbitrary URLs. For vendor-operated renderers, the evidence is tenant configuration plus provider documentation or the organization's own tests.
evidence: Renderer or tenant configuration showing remote-content fetching and unfurls disabled or limited to listed origins; quarterly allowlist review record with removed entries; test results showing canary data in Markdown, reference-style and invisible-Unicode link variants is not fetched.
guidance: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) leaked Copilot data through an auto-fetched image. CamoLeak (2025) used GitHub's image proxy, and the fix was to disable image rendering. ForcedLeak (2025) used an expired allowlisted domain bought for about $5. Data can also travel in subdomains (DNS) and paths, so prefer inert links. OWASP LLM10:2026 recommends auto-rendering off by default. BAL-5.4 tests these cases for built assets; BAL-8.6 adds vendor evidence at T2.

requirement: User input, and every input path through which the asset accepts content the user did not author (retrieved documents, tool and MCP output, fetched web pages, email, and text extracted from images or documents), is screened by a detector for defined families of instruction-override and jailbreak attempts. Detections are logged as security events (BAL-7.3) and handled by a response defined for the asset: block, strip the content, or downgrade the session so that it can no longer write or send data externally. This detection is a tripwire and does not satisfy BAL-6.1 or BAL-3.5.
evidence: Detector configuration covering user input and each untrusted input path in the threat model; the documented response for the asset; sample security events in the monitoring platform showing the response taken.
guidance: Cover known jailbreak families: role-play, payload splitting, encoding and obfuscation, and low-resource languages. For agents, prefer downgrade-to-read-only so false positives do not break work. Expect bypass: EchoLeak got past a production injection classifier, and in ShareLeak the request was reportedly flagged yet data still left. On vendor platforms, enable built-in detection and record its response. Test with BAL-5.3 and BAL-5.4 cases; BAL-5.11 and BAL-5.9 measure efficacy at T2.

requirement: System prompts, tool schemas, agent memory and other context hidden from the user contain no credentials, tokens or connection strings, and no authorization or policy logic whose enforcement depends on that context staying secret. Every entitlement or restriction that hidden context describes is also enforced in code or configuration outside the model, so disclosing hidden context grants no access and bypasses no restriction.
evidence: Secret-scan results for system prompts, templates and tool schemas; review record mapping each restriction in hidden context to the control that enforces it outside the model; extraction test showing disclosed context yields no credentials or bypass.
guidance: Assume hidden context can be extracted (ATLAS AML.T0056; OWASP LLM08:2026 Hidden Context Exposure). An instruction such as 'do not reveal these instructions' is not a control. Scan prompts, templates and tool schemas for secrets in the same pipeline as code; BAL-2.4 already bars credentials from model context. Handle business-confidential prompt content under BAL-4.1, not as a security boundary.

requirement: Permitted and restricted topics and intents are defined for the asset from its approved purpose. Prompts are classified against them, and restricted requests are refused or routed to an approved channel according to a documented policy.
evidence: Topic and intent policy for the asset derived from its registered purpose; classifier or routing configuration; test results or sampled logs showing restricted requests refused or routed.
guidance: Useful for public-facing and regulated assets, for example to keep a claims assistant out of legal or medical advice. It narrows misuse and supports intended-use obligations, but it is not an injection defense. Take the purpose from intake (BAL-1.6) and include the classifier in guardrail efficacy measurement (BAL-5.11).

requirement: Before untrusted input reaches the model, its tools or a code interpreter, it is screened for known-bad URLs, executable or encoded payloads and malicious attachments, and every modality the asset accepts (images, audio, video and documents, including hidden layers, metadata and embedded objects) is screened for embedded instructions. Detections are handled under the response defined in BAL-6.4.
evidence: Inspection pipeline configuration listing each accepted modality; test results for instructions hidden in an image, an audio clip and a document's hidden text; logs of detections handled under the BAL-6.4 response.
guidance: Covers what text-only inspection misses: instructions in image pixels, QR codes, audio, white or tiny text, comments, alt text, metadata and hidden sheets. ATLAS AML.T0129 (2026.09) describes triggers placed in a modality that defenses do not inspect. Decode common encodings before inspection. Reuse existing malware and URL-reputation services; the AI-specific delta is inspecting every modality before it becomes model context.

requirement: Output of user-facing generative assets is scored against defined harm categories, including violent, sexual, self-harm, extremist, hateful and discriminatory content. It is blocked, modified or escalated according to thresholds set for the asset's audience and purpose.
evidence: Harm-category policy with thresholds for the asset; output filter configuration on the response path; test results or sampled logs showing blocked, modified and escalated outputs with reviewer decisions.
guidance: Primarily a safety and brand control. Set stricter thresholds for public or vulnerable audiences. Jailbreaks target this filter, so pair it with BAL-6.4 and include it in guardrail efficacy measurement (BAL-5.11).

requirement: Outputs used to support decisions are scored for grounding against the context retrieved for them. Responses below a defined threshold are flagged to the user or withheld, and the score is recorded with the response.
evidence: Groundedness scoring configuration and threshold for each decision-support use; validation results supporting the chosen threshold; sampled responses showing recorded scores and the flag shown to users.
guidance: A reliability and misinformation control (OWASP LLM07:2026). A poisoned source still yields a well-grounded answer, so this does not replace source trust labeling (BAL-4.9), content labeling (BAL-6.2) or retrieval-generated citations (BAL-4.12). Decision support includes eligibility, pricing, claims, HR and security triage. Set the threshold from validation on the asset's own test set.

control: Safe handling of model output by interpreters
requirement: Model output passed to a shell, code interpreter, database query, template engine or web page is treated as untrusted input. Commands and queries are parameterized or validated against an allowlist of permitted operations, and output inserted into HTML or other markup is encoded for its context. Generated code or commands that cannot be validated run only inside the isolation boundary of BAL-6.13, so injected code, queries or commands do not execute with the asset's own privileges.
evidence: Design or code review record of parameterization, encoding or sandboxing at each point where model output reaches an interpreter; test results with injected SQL, shell and script payloads in model output; database role or sandbox configuration used.
guidance: The AI form of downstream injection (OWASP LLM10:2026, ASI05). Examples: text-to-SQL through read-only roles or parameterized views with row limits; no eval or shell=True on model output; context encoding to prevent script injection in agent-built pages. Vendor coding agents typically meet this through BAL-6.13 sandboxing. Commit-time scanning of generated code is BAL-5.22.

requirement: Structured model output consumed by downstream systems, other than tool-call arguments (BAL-3.2), is validated before use against a defined schema, including types, ranges and allowed values. Output that fails validation is rejected or routed for handling rather than passed on.
evidence: Schema for each structured output consumed downstream; validator configuration at the consuming boundary; test results or logs showing malformed or out-of-range outputs rejected and routed for handling.
guidance: Covers extracted fields, classifications and decisions that feed workflows, APIs or other agents. A provider's structured-output mode reduces malformed output but does not replace validation by the consumer. Validation limits how far a manipulated or faulty response can travel (ASI08).

requirement: The agent runtime or platform enforces hard limits, outside the model, on steps, wall-clock time, tool calls, recursion depth and spawned sub-agents per task. Repeating the same action without progress beyond a defined count counts as exceeding a limit. Exceeding any limit terminates the task, leaves in-flight work in a defined state, and is logged.
evidence: Runtime or platform configuration showing limits for each agent; test showing a looping or over-long task is terminated; log entries for terminated tasks naming the limit exceeded.
guidance: Suggested starting defaults, tuned per workflow: 50 tool calls and 30 minutes for interactive tasks, recursion depth 3, five sub-agents, and three identical calls without new results. Limits come from the agent's registration, not its prompt. Automatic halting across tasks is BAL-3.11 and per-agent budgets are BAL-3.10 (both T2); provider spend ceilings are BAL-3.8. ATLAS AML.M0036 covers similar resource bounds.

requirement: Every tool path the agent uses, including file reads, runs inside an isolation boundary enforced outside the agent: a virtual machine, microVM or hardened container for unattended agents or any action class at A3 or above, and at least an operating-system sandbox for interactive agents; command allowlists alone do not satisfy this. Inside the boundary no ambient credentials are readable (cloud CLI profiles, SSH keys, browser cookie stores, package-publishing tokens, environment secrets, instance metadata), writes are limited to the task workspace and exclude agent configuration, hooks and shell profiles, and network access follows BAL-6.14. Coding agents hold no production, cloud-administration or package-publishing credentials, and autonomous testing and evaluation agents are in scope. For vendor-operated runtimes, provider documentation of the boundary plus the organization's runtime settings is the evidence.
evidence: Sandbox or VM configuration per agent showing filesystem, credential and network boundaries; test results in which the agent tries to read credential files, instance metadata and its own configuration and is denied; credential inventory showing coding agents hold no production or publishing tokens.
guidance: The Claude Code GitHub Action's file-read tool sat outside its shell sandbox, and injected instructions read /proc/self/environ to expose an API key (Microsoft, June 2026). METR (August 2026) traced evaluation agents reaching Hugging Face through a package proxy and an internet-connected sandbox. Build each run from a clean image (ATLAS AML.M0032), broker credentials where possible (BAL-2.11, T2) and test for escapes. Ambient credentials are those the task does not need (developer and machine credentials); the agent's own task credentials are governed by BAL-2.4, and brokering them outside the agent's reach is the T2 control BAL-2.11.

requirement: Network egress from agent runtimes and sandboxes, including MCP servers the agent launches, is denied by default and allowed only to listed destinations. It is enforced at a layer the agent cannot reconfigure, and names are resolved only through the enforcing proxy or a filtering resolver, with no direct DNS. Listed hosts that serve user-generated content, pastes, open redirects or generic proxies are excluded or restricted to specific paths, allowlists are reviewed on a defined cadence and monitored for domain expiry and ownership change, and autonomous testing agents are limited to an enforced target allowlist. For vendor-operated runtimes, the evidence is the platform's egress settings plus provider documentation of server-side enforcement.
evidence: Egress proxy or firewall policy for agent runtimes showing default deny and the allowlist; test results showing direct DNS and unlisted destinations blocked from inside the sandbox; allowlist review and domain-expiry monitoring records.
guidance: In CVE-2025-55284, auto-approved ping and nslookup let a coding agent exfiltrate .env contents through DNS. ForcedLeak shows why listed domains need expiry monitoring. Suggested cadence: quarterly review, with daily expiry and ownership checks. Exfiltration through rendering in the user's client is BAL-6.3. Restricting allowed multi-tenant services to the organization's own accounts is BAL-6.15 (T2).

requirement: Multi-tenant destinations on an agent egress allowlist, such as model provider APIs, code hosts, storage and SaaS services, accept only the organization's own tenants, accounts or keys. This is enforced at the egress layer or by the destination service, so data cannot be sent to an attacker-owned account on an allowed host.
evidence: List of allowed multi-tenant destinations with the restriction mechanism for each; proxy or gateway rules enforcing tenant or account restriction; test showing a request carrying a foreign API key or tenant is blocked.
guidance: In the Claude Cowork case reported by PromptArmor, the sandbox blocked most domains but allowed the model provider's API, and an injected command uploaded files using the attacker's API key. Mechanisms include tenant-restriction headers at the proxy, credential injection that replaces any caller-supplied key, and rules scoped by account or path for code hosts and storage.

requirement: For coding assistants and endpoint agents: (a) agents cannot write their own approval or permission settings, which are protected by file permissions or the sandbox, and agent writes to their own configuration, instruction files, MCP server definitions or hooks are blocked or need per-change user approval enforced outside the model; (b) permission-bypass and auto-approve modes are disabled through managed settings that neither user nor agent can change, stored where ownership and permissions are verified, except in approved disposable sandboxes; (c) repository-supplied configuration that can execute code or change permissions loads only after workspace trust is granted, and trust is re-requested when that content changes; (d) changes to agent instruction and configuration files in organization repositories require code-owner review and are scanned for hidden or bidirectional Unicode; (e) deviations from the managed baseline, and unauthenticated or network-exposed agent control interfaces, are detected and remediated within a defined period.
evidence: Managed settings deployed to endpoints with bypass and auto-approve disabled and file ownership verified; workspace-trust test using a repository with a malicious hook; baseline-drift and exposed-interface reports with remediation records.
guidance: In CVE-2025-53773, an injected coding agent switched on auto-approve in workspace settings. In CVE-2026-35603, a managed-settings file in a user-writable location let low-privileged users plant configuration. s1ngularity (2025) malware invoked AI CLIs with bypass flags. Repository-supplied configuration includes hooks, MCP definitions, agent settings and dev-container files. Prefer stdio for local MCP servers. Suggested remediation period: 5 business days. Endpoint discovery of these tools is BAL-1.9. Vendor classifier-based or 'auto' modes that execute actions without per-action approval count as auto-approve modes: disabled on managed endpoints, or used only in approved disposable sandboxes after a promotion gate (BAL-3.1).

control: AI platform and SaaS tenant configuration baseline
requirement: Security-relevant settings of AI platforms and SaaS AI tenants have an approved baseline per user group. The baseline covers at least: agent creation, publishing and sharing; public or broad sharing of conversations, outputs and custom assistants; agent discovery and autonomous execution, with agent discovery and cross-agent delegation off unless approved; connectors and outbound actions such as HTTP requests and email; memory; web access; output rendering and allowed-URL lists; meeting and ambient-capture AI; and administrator and agent-maker role assignments, separated as BAL-1.2 requires. Deviations from the baseline are detected and remediated within a defined period.
evidence: Approved baseline for each AI platform and SaaS tenant per user group; configuration assessment comparing live settings with the baseline; remediation records for deviations closed within the defined period.
guidance: Incidents came from tenant defaults. ServiceNow Now Assist agents were discoverable and grouped into one team by default (AppOmni, 2025), and Agentforce enforced Trusted URLs only after ForcedLeak. Start from vendor baselines, with agent discovery, cross-agent delegation and public sharing off unless approved. Role separation follows BAL-1.2. Suggested: assess monthly and after vendor feature notices (BAL-8.8); remediate within 30 days, or 72 hours for settings that expose data publicly.

requirement: Input, output and tool-call policy is enforced at a gateway, proxy or platform boundary that application code cannot bypass because routing, access and credential restrictions are enforced outside that code. SDK middleware alone does not meet this requirement. Tool and MCP traffic fails closed when required enforcement is unavailable. Model traffic may use a documented fallback only while all mandatory controls remain enforced; otherwise it fails closed. Direct bypass calls are denied, and attempts are investigated using enforcement logs, egress telemetry and BAL-1.8 reconciliation.
evidence: Routing and credential restrictions showing that application code cannot bypass the enforcement point; direct-bypass and outage tests proving tool/MCP denial and preservation of mandatory model controls; provider-usage reconciliation with investigated bypass attempts.
guidance: Prevents a new code path or developer shortcut from skipping BAL-3.2 and BAL-6.4 checks. Issue provider keys only to the enforcement point so direct calls fail, and reconcile provider usage against its logs. A model fallback uses an alternative enforcement path that continues to satisfy all mandatory controls; otherwise model traffic fails closed. Tool and MCP traffic always fails closed when required enforcement is unavailable. When self-hosted, the enforcement point is a critical asset under BAL-6.19.

control: Self-hosted AI service exposure and hardening
requirement: Self-hosted AI services (inference servers, AI gateways, agent and workflow builders, MCP servers, vector databases, and notebook and ML control planes) are registered as AI assets (BAL-1.6) with owner, version and network exposure. Every interface requires authentication, with no default or anonymous access, and no such service is reachable from the internet unless that exposure is approved at intake (BAL-1.6) and recorded with the asset, as for the public interface of a PUBLIC asset. The services are covered by external attack-surface monitoring and vulnerability management, with known-exploited vulnerabilities in AI frameworks, SDKs and agent runtimes fixed within the organization's remediation timeline for known-exploited vulnerabilities, and administrative access requires phishing-resistant MFA. AI gateways and guardrail services are classified at the organization's highest asset criticality.
evidence: Inventory of self-hosted AI services with owner and exposure status; external attack-surface scan showing no unapproved internet-reachable AI service; vulnerability records showing KEV-listed AI framework fixes within the timeline.
guidance: Langflow CVE-2026-33017, an unauthenticated RCE, was exploited within about 20 hours of disclosure and added to CISA KEV. Researchers counted about 175,000 publicly exposed Ollama hosts in January 2026. Model endpoints are inventoried under BAL-1.8 and components of built assets under BAL-1.7; this control adds exposure for every self-hosted AI service. Suggested KEV timeline: the CISA KEV due date. Treat gateways as tier-0 because every guardrail depends on them.

requirement: AI browsers and browser agent modes, including agentic features in mainstream browsers and extensions, are blocked by default on managed endpoints and are excluded from the graduated response in BAL-8.10. A product or mode is approved only when configuration or provider evidence shows that: (a) agent tasks run in a separate profile or container that does not inherit the user's authenticated corporate sessions, or are limited to approved sites; (b) the user explicitly confirms before the agent enters credentials, makes payments, submits forms, downloads files or moves data between sites; and (c) agent actions are logged (BAL-7.1).
evidence: Browser and application management policy blocking AI browsers and agent modes; approval record for any permitted product showing profile isolation or site limits and confirmation settings; sample agent action logs.
guidance: Agentic browsers act inside the user's sessions while reading arbitrary pages. In CometJacking (LayerX, 2025), one crafted URL led to exfiltration of mail and calendar data. CSO Online reported in December 2025 that Gartner analysts advised blocking AI browsers. Enforce this through browser and application management, and find unapproved AI browsers through endpoint discovery (BAL-1.9). Desktop computer-use agents are covered by BAL-6.13.

requirement: Agent discovery and delegation are disabled by default, and permitted caller-to-callee paths are explicitly allowlisted (on SaaS platforms, by segmenting agents). Each caller verifies the receiving endpoint's identity, and each receiving agent authenticates every request using verifiable caller credentials tied to its approved identity (BAL-2.1), then authorizes the requested capability. Signed, pinned agent descriptors protect discovery metadata but do not replace request authentication. Delegated authority only narrows along the chain (BAL-2.3, BAL-2.12), output from another agent is handled as untrusted content (BAL-6.2), and the kill switch (BAL-3.7) can halt the whole chain.
evidence: Register of permitted agent-to-agent paths with discovery settings; caller-credential and peer-identity verification configuration; negative tests showing that a copied valid descriptor does not authorize a request with invalid credentials, and that an unlisted call is refused; a test showing halt propagation down the chain.
guidance: AppOmni (November 2025) showed second-order injection between ServiceNow agents that were discoverable by default. Signed Agent Cards in A2A v1.0.1 provide discovery-metadata authenticity and integrity; the protocol's separate request-authentication requirements still apply. Authentication does not stop injected content from propagating, so the receiving agent's own controls (BAL-6.1, BAL-3.5) still apply. For all assets, the BAL-6.17 baseline also covers agent discovery settings.

requirement: A component outside the model tracks the agent's plan and data flows, so that values derived from untrusted sources cannot reach sensitive sinks, including recipients, destinations, code execution and permission changes, without passing an explicit policy check enforced outside the model. Tracking covers values that pass through intermediate tool results.
evidence: Design record of the provenance-tracking mechanism and its sink policies; test results where untrusted values are blocked at each sensitive sink; policy decision logs showing provenance labels on evaluated values.
guidance: Two patterns. In CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813), a privileged planner sees only the trusted request, a quarantined model handles untrusted data, and an interpreter enforces policy at each tool call. FIDES (arXiv 2505.23643) applies confidentiality and integrity labels to messages and tool results. Expect a utility cost: CaMeL completed 77% of AgentDojo tasks against 84% undefended. Guarantees do not automatically compose across agent hierarchies.

requirement: Every agent action (tool or MCP call, file access, shell command, outbound request, model or configuration change, plugin or skill invocation) is logged by the enforcement point that executes or mediates it, not from the model's own account. Neither the agent nor its owner can modify or delete the records. Each record identifies the invoking user, agent identity and delegation chain, host or device, model, tool or server and its version, target, decision and rule applied, and a correlation ID linking prompt, response and tool calls. Records are kept apart from prompt and response logs for a defined minimum period. Vendor-operated agents meet this through the vendor's audit log, enabled and exported.
evidence: Sample action records from the gateway, MCP proxy, sandbox or platform audit log showing every required field; access configuration showing the agent and its owner cannot alter or delete records; retention setting of the log store.
guidance: Suggested default: 180 days, or longer where law or contract requires; this is a Ballast baseline, not an EU AI Act figure. METR's August 2026 investigation found spoofed tool calls in roughly 7% of evaluated transcripts (an evaluation setting, not a base rate), so model narratives are not evidence. Endpoint agents ship records off-device promptly. For vendor-operated agents, an absent or disabled vendor audit log blocks production use (BAL-7.1 is non-acceptable); individual missing fields are recorded as Partially implemented with a request to the vendor. Prompt content in records follows BAL-4.4. Richer provenance: BAL-7.11.

requirement: Logs and traces that capture prompts, responses, retrieved context or tool inputs and outputs are classified at the highest sensitivity of data they can contain and encrypted at rest and in transit, including copies held in observability and evaluation tools and in vendor admin or eDiscovery stores. Raw content is readable only by named roles, and every raw read or export is itself logged. Retention and deletion follow BAL-4.4.
evidence: Inventory of stores holding prompt or response content (application logs, traces, observability tools, vendor stores) with their classification; named-role list for raw access; sample audit entries showing raw reads and exports being logged.
guidance: LLM tracing, observability and evaluation tools, support bundles and vendor compliance stores often hold full prompts, including pasted secrets, so inventory them all. A user viewing their own conversation history, including transcripts a coding agent keeps on their device, is not a raw read; such local transcripts still need device encryption and BAL-4.4 retention. Redaction before write, customer-managed keys and tamper evidence are in BAL-7.10 (T2, informative).

control: AI security event forwarding and telemetry health
requirement: AI security events (guardrail detections, policy blocks and escalations, approval decisions, kill-switch use, spend alerts) and administrative changes to AI platforms, guardrails and agent configurations are forwarded to the security monitoring platform, where AI platform administrators cannot alter them. Each event type has a severity, an accountable owner and a triage runbook. Each inventoried AI asset is mapped to its telemetry sources, with gaps closed or accepted under BAL-1.13, and loss or disabling of a source raises an alert. Where AI agents close alerts, which BAL-3.6 allows only with per-action approval or within limits pre-authorized at the promotion gate (BAL-3.1), a human reviews a defined sample of agent-closed alerts, and agents are denied permission to close alerts about their own identity or actions.
evidence: Event-type catalog with severity, owner and triage runbook; AI asset to telemetry-source coverage map with gap dispositions, plus a record of a telemetry-loss alert; review log for sampled agent-closed alerts and the permission setting that blocks self-closure.
guidance: Event schemas (for example OCSF) and response automation are implementation choices. Telemetry-health checks should also catch agents started with auditing or permission checks disabled (ATLAS AML.T0081). Suggested defaults: alert when expected heartbeats or event volume are missing for 1 hour on continuously used gateways and agent runtimes, or 24 hours on vendor audit feeds; human review of at least 5% of agent-closed alerts. Attack-chain detections: BAL-7.12 (T2, where implemented).

requirement: The incident response plan includes AI-specific playbooks, each with triggers, an accountable owner and response steps, for at least: injection-driven data exfiltration; compromised agent or AI-integration credentials or OAuth grants; malicious or modified models, MCP servers, skills, plugins or extensions; poisoned retrieval indexes or agent memory; runaway or destructive agent actions; and vulnerabilities or breaches disclosed by AI vendors. Each playbook defines: containment (BAL-3.7); revocation, within a defined time, of every token, grant and key the affected agent or integration held (BAL-2.4, BAL-2.7); preservation of prompts, retrieved context, tool-call chains and memory and index snapshots before any purge; impact scoping across the full exposure window; purge or rollback to a known-good state; and notification decisions for regulators, clients, providers and affected users against applicable deadlines. A published channel receives external vulnerability reports about the organization's AI features. Playbooks are exercised at least annually.
evidence: AI playbooks with triggers, owner and steps for each listed scenario; latest exercise record with measured halt and revocation times and lessons learned; published vulnerability-reporting channel that covers AI features.
guidance: Informative: CoSAI AI Incident Response Framework v1.0 (Oct 2025); OWASP GenAI Incident Response Guide 1.0 (Jul 2025). Salesloft Drift (Aug 2025) shows revocation must reach every grant an AI vendor holds, across platforms, at once. BAL-1.2 names the AI incident lead; BAL-8.4 sets vendor notification terms; rollback uses BAL-4.14 where implemented. EU AI Act Art. 73 reporting applies only to high-risk systems (Annex III obligations from 2 Dec 2027).

requirement: Each agent identity, including the identity of any third-party AI app connected to organizational data, has an expected activity profile covering tools, call rates, data sources, data volumes, targets and active hours. The profile is derived from the agent's declared purpose and autonomy envelope (BAL-3.1) or from an observed baseline. Deviations beyond defined thresholds, including bulk queries or exports through connected AI apps, raise alerts that are triaged within a defined time. For agents under BAL-3.11, defined alert types trip the circuit breaker automatically.
evidence: Activity profiles and thresholds for a sample of agents and AI-integration identities; alert records with triage timestamps; configuration showing which alert types trip the BAL-3.11 circuit breaker.
guidance: An A3 agent's declared envelope (BAL-3.1) is a ready-made profile; learned baselines suit high-volume integrations. Typical deviations: first use of a tool, a new destination domain, record volumes far above baseline, off-hours activity, or a third-party AI app's OAuth client exporting whole object tables (the Salesloft Drift pattern, 2025). Suggested triage times: 1 hour for alerts on Critical assets, 4 hours on High assets.

requirement: Sessions, outputs and agent tasks that retrieve or assemble sensitive data beyond a defined per-data-class volume threshold within a defined time window are detected, even when the requester is entitled to every item individually. Thresholds are set for each data class the asset can reach, and they count activity across sessions by the same user or agent.
evidence: Per-data-class thresholds and time windows for the asset; detection rule or configuration; test record showing an alert when an entitled user or agent exceeded a threshold through individually permitted requests.
guidance: Example thresholds: more than 50 personal-data records, or more than 20 documents labeled restricted, per user or agent per hour. Each retrieval may be authorized while the total is not, so permission checks (BAL-4.7) do not catch this. BAL-4.8 fixes over-broad grounding scope; this control catches what remains.

requirement: Usage of each approved tool server, MCP server, skill and plugin is tracked (invoking agents and users, call volume, last use) and feeds capability classification (BAL-3.3), component review (BAL-5.16) and catalog maintenance (BAL-5.18). Components unused for a defined period are flagged for removal, and changes beyond defined thresholds in a component's call or response pattern after approval are flagged for re-review.
evidence: Usage report per tool server, MCP server, skill and plugin showing invoking agents, users, volume and last use; records of components flagged as unused or changed and the resulting review or removal.
guidance: Gateway, MCP proxy or platform logs are adequate sources. Suggested defaults: flag components unused for 90 days, and flag a tenfold change in call volume or response size or responses that reference new external domains. Remote MCP servers can change behavior without changing their definitions (ATLAS AML.T0109, rug pull), so usage signals add to the fingerprinting in BAL-5.17.

requirement: Every allow, block, redact or escalate decision by a guardrail or policy enforcement point is recorded with: the rule or detector that fired and its version; the policy version; the score and threshold where a classifier decided; and references to the inputs evaluated rather than copies of them. Records are queryable and exportable, and any input content they hold is protected as in BAL-7.2.
evidence: Sample decision records showing rule or detector, versions, score, threshold and input references; a query or export of decisions for a date range; check that records contain no unprotected prompt content.
guidance: Most injection and leakage guardrails are classifiers with no rule to report, so record detector, version, score and threshold instead. Store references (hashes, record IDs) to evaluated inputs, not copies, so decision logs do not become an unprotected second prompt log. Decision records also feed guardrail efficacy measurement (BAL-5.11). BAL-7.1 already sets the minimum decision fields for agent actions.

requirement: For any alert or reported incident involving the asset, authorized investigators can reconstruct within a defined time the prompts, retrieved context (or versioned references to it), model and configuration versions, responses, memory reads and writes, and tool-call chain behind it, linked by correlation identifiers. BAL-4.4 retention for these records covers a defined investigation look-back period. Reconstruction time is verified in the BAL-7.4 exercises.
evidence: Investigation runbook naming data sources and correlation keys; exercise record reconstructing an alert's full chain within the defined time; sample reconstruction output.
guidance: Suggested defaults: reconstruction within 4 hours for Critical and 1 business day for High assets; look-back matching the BAL-7.1 retention where privacy rules allow. Store retrieved-chunk IDs with the index version, and snapshot memory when an alert fires. Vendor-operated agents depend on vendor exports (BAL-8.6). In July 2026, OpenAI took about a week to establish that its own evaluation agents caused the Hugging Face intrusion.

requirement: Sensitive data classes in prompt and response logs are redacted or reversibly tokenized before they are written. Detokenization is restricted to authorized investigators and is itself logged. The logs are encrypted with customer-managed keys where the platform supports them and held in tamper-evident storage.
evidence: Redaction or tokenization configuration with sample log entries; detokenization access list and its audit log; key-management and tamper-evidence configuration, or a record that customer-managed keys are unavailable.
guidance: Reversible tokenization keeps investigation possible (BAL-7.9) while removing raw sensitive values from routine log access. Not every SaaS AI service offers customer-managed keys; record where they are unavailable. Tamper evidence can use write-once storage or hash chaining. Redaction rules should cover the data classes defined under BAL-4.1.

requirement: In addition to the BAL-7.1 fields, each agent action record carries: a hash of the tool definition as presented to the model; the subject and actor token identifiers; the untrusted sources present in context when the action was chosen; any memory writes; and each agent-to-agent hop. Records are correlated across services by propagated trace context and held in tamper-evident storage.
evidence: Sample action records with tool-definition hash, subject and actor token identifiers, untrusted context sources, memory writes and agent hops; one cross-service trace for a multi-step task; tamper-evident storage configuration.
guidance: Propagate trace IDs with W3C Trace Context or the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions across gateways, MCP servers and sub-agents. The tool-definition hash shows whether a tool changed between approval (BAL-5.17) and use. Recording untrusted context sources lets responders trace an action back to the injected document or email. Log token identifiers (for example the jti claim), not the tokens themselves.

requirement: The security monitoring platform carries maintained detections for AI attack chains, each mapped to MITRE ATLAS technique IDs and reviewed at least quarterly. At minimum they cover: sensitive data encoded in outbound URLs or rendered links; memory writes in sessions that ingested untrusted content; agents launched with approval or sandbox bypass settings, or AI agent CLIs started by unexpected parent processes; changes to MCP tool definitions after approval; agent processes reading credential stores or agent configuration secrets; and bulk export by AI-integration identities.
evidence: Detection inventory mapped to ATLAS IDs with last review date; test results showing each minimum detection fired on replayed attack data; quarterly review record with changes made.
guidance: ATLAS 2026.09 IDs for the minimum set: AML.T0077, AML.T0086 (encoded data); AML.T0080.000 (memory writes); AML.T0103, AML.T0081 (bypass flags or unexpected parents, as in the s1ngularity/Nx attack of Aug 2025, which ran AI CLIs with permission checks disabled); AML.T0109 (definition change); AML.T0083, AML.T0098 (credential reads). Validate detections by replaying BAL-5.3 and BAL-5.4 test cases, and pin them to the ATLAS release.

requirement: Decoy credentials, documents, retrieval entries, tools or endpoints are placed where no legitimate user, agent or task has reason to touch them, so any use indicates a compromised or misbehaving agent or an attacker. Any use raises a high-severity alert handled under BAL-7.4. Decoys are registered so responders and inventories recognize them.
evidence: Decoy register with locations and owners; alert rule for each decoy; test record showing a decoy touch produced a high-severity alert handled under BAL-7.4.
guidance: ATLAS AML.M0039 AI Honeypots (added in release 2026.09). Examples: a decoy API key in an agent-readable configuration file; a canary document in a retrieval index that normal queries do not match; a decoy high-value tool no legitimate task needs. Decoys grant no real access, and decoy tools are described so benign agents are not drawn to them. Unlike the BAL-5.4 test canaries, these run in production.

requirement: An externally sourced model, including adapters and embedding models, is assessed against organization-defined acceptance criteria before it is ingested and before each new version is adopted. The criteria cover publisher identity and namespace ownership, adoption and reputation, license and use terms, artifact scan results (BAL-5.12), known vulnerabilities and incidents, and available model documentation. The decision, approver and assessed revision are recorded, and a model that does not meet the criteria is not ingested. Models used only through a provider API are profiled under BAL-8.7 instead.
evidence: Completed assessment for a recently ingested model showing each criterion, the decision, approver and assessed revision; AI bill of materials or model registry entry linking the assessment to the pinned revision; a rejected model with the recorded reason.
guidance: Reputation signals can be manufactured (AML.T0111), and deleted publisher namespaces can be re-registered (Unit 42 'model namespace reuse', Sep 2025). Do not let reputation alone pass a model: verify the namespace owner and pin the assessed revision (BAL-5.14). Useful documentation includes model cards and, for general-purpose models, EU AI Act Art. 53 documentation. For assets the organization builds, link the assessment from the AI bill of materials (BAL-1.7).

requirement: The contract or binding service terms for each AI vendor prohibit use of the organization's prompts, outputs, uploaded files and connected data to train, fine-tune or evaluate the vendor's or any third party's models, including for product improvement. At onboarding and at a defined interval after, the organization verifies that every organizational account, plan and setting it uses with that vendor falls under the commitment. Any that do not are reconfigured, migrated or closed.
evidence: Contract, data processing agreement or service-terms clause prohibiting training use; tenant or account settings export showing plan type and training use disabled; reconciliation of provider accounts in the usage inventory (BAL-1.8) against plans covered by the commitment.
guidance: Consumer and commercial terms can differ sharply. From late August 2025, Anthropic's consumer plans asked users to choose whether chats train models, with five-year retention for those who agree; commercial and API terms were unchanged. Personal accounts carry consumer terms into work (BAL-8.9). Check whether feedback features carry different rights. Abuse-monitoring review is not training use; BAL-8.7 profiles its retention. Suggested interval: annually.

control: Vendor data isolation, retention and deletion
requirement: Each AI vendor evidences three things for the services the organization uses: (a) isolation of the organization's data from other customers by tenant, region and model, including in vendor-hosted agent runtimes, code-execution sandboxes, connectors, MCP servers and the shared internal services they rely on; (b) retention periods and deletion across primary storage, backups, logs and safety or abuse-monitoring stores; and (c) exit terms for return of the organization's data and for confirmed deletion on request, at exit and at decommissioning (BAL-1.15).
evidence: Vendor isolation documentation or assurance-report section covering agent runtimes, sandboxes and connectors; retention schedule per store, including abuse-monitoring stores; exit and deletion clause, with a deletion confirmation from an offboarded vendor or decommissioned asset.
guidance: Cross-tenant failures now occur in AI infrastructure. A bug in Asana's MCP server exposed about 1,000 customers' data to other MCP users (Jun 2025). A shared internal artifact repository behind ChatGPT code-execution containers let instructions reach other accounts' data (Check Point, Sep 2026). Safety stores can outlive stated retention: Microsoft documents one model provider keeping flagged content up to 2 years and classifier scores up to 7.

control: Vendor incident notification, sub-processors and audit rights
requirement: AI vendor contracts require three things. (a) Notification of security incidents affecting the organization's data or AI services, within a period that lets the organization meet its shortest applicable regulatory or contractual deadline. This explicitly includes exploited prompt injection, cross-tenant exposure through AI features, model or agent compromise, and vendor-fixed vulnerabilities that may have exposed the organization's data. (b) Disclosure of underlying model providers and other sub-processors, with advance notice of changes and a right to object. (c) A right to audit, or a commitment to provide independent assurance reports in its place (BAL-8.5).
evidence: Executed contract or data processing agreement clauses on notification period, AI-specific incident scope, sub-processor notice and objection, and audit or assurance rights; mapping of the notification period to the shortest applicable deadline; current sub-processor list naming underlying model providers.
guidance: Derive the period from the shortest clock that applies, for example GDPR Art. 33 or NYDFS Part 500 (72 hours), or DORA major-incident reporting. Suggested default: 24 hours from vendor awareness. EchoLeak (Jun 2025) was fixed server-side with no customer action; only notice lets customers search their own logs for the exposure window (BAL-7.4). BAL-8.8 monitors model-change and retirement notices.

requirement: Each AI vendor holds current independent assurance whose scope covers the AI services and features the organization uses. At onboarding and at each renewal, the organization reviews the assurance for four things: scope; exclusions and carve-outs, including carved-out sub-processors such as underlying model providers; exceptions noted by the assessor; and the customer responsibilities the report assigns. Each gap is recorded with a compensating control or a BAL-1.13 exception.
evidence: Current certificate or report per AI vendor with a scope statement covering the AI features in use; review record noting carve-outs, assessor exceptions and customer responsibilities; gap entries with compensating controls or exception references.
guidance: AI-specific options include ISO/IEC 42001 certification from an accredited body; CSA STAR for AI Level 2 (third-party assurance of AI security controls; verify the certification route and scope; Level 1 is a self-assessment); AIUC-1 (a third-party-audited AI agent certification valid for one year); and HITRUST AI Security. SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 cover general controls but often exclude new AI features. Carry assigned customer responsibilities into the tenant baseline (BAL-6.17).

requirement: This control applies to each AI service where the vendor operates the agent runtime, tool or connector execution, outbound requests or output rendering. The organization reviews evidence of the vendor's defenses against prompt injection and data exfiltration: separation of untrusted content from instructions and authority, output rendering and URL limits, server-side egress controls and approval of high-risk actions. It records which agent actions and outbound requests it can export to its own logs (BAL-7.1). Gaps have compensating controls or a BAL-1.13 exception. The review is repeated at a defined interval and after material vendor change (BAL-8.8).
evidence: Evidence pack per vendor service (security documentation, test or red-team summaries, configuration options) with reviewer notes against each defense; matrix of agent actions and outbound requests exportable to the organization's logs; gap entries with compensating controls or exception IDs.
guidance: Enterprise controls cannot see what runs on the vendor side. ShadowLeak (2025) leaked mailbox data directly from the vendor's cloud. ForcedLeak (Agentforce, CVSS 9.4, 2025) exfiltrated to an expired allowlisted domain until trusted-URL enforcement shipped. For High and Critical assets, this review is the evidence route for the vendor-side enforcement points of BAL-3.5, 3.6, 6.3, 6.4 and 7.1. Prefer test results scoped to the features you enable. Suggested interval: annually.

control: AI vendor, plan and model risk profiling
requirement: Each AI vendor, each commercial plan and each model offered within a plan is profiled for: training use of customer data; retention, including abuse-monitoring retention; zero-data-retention availability; data residency and boundary coverage; and processing role, including whether a model runs under another provider's terms. The profile states the data classes it permits. A model or plan is enabled for users only when its profile permits the data classes those users handle. Organizational accounts on plans that permit no organizational data are migrated or closed; personal use of such plans is handled under BAL-8.9 and BAL-8.10.
evidence: Profile register listing each vendor, plan and model with the profiled attributes and permitted data classes; enablement record showing a model or plan approved against its profile; migration or closure record for an organizational account on a disallowed plan.
guidance: Terms now differ per model, not just per vendor. From 9 Jun 2026, Anthropic retains data for Mythos-class models for 30 days with no zero-data-retention option. Microsoft enables Anthropic models by default for most commercial tenants outside the EU, EFTA and UK, excluded from its EU Data Boundary; variants with data retention are opt-in and run under Anthropic's own terms (Sep 2026). Profiles feed BAL-8.10 and BAL-4.6; BAL-8.8 keeps them current.

requirement: A named owner monitors and risk-assesses vendor notices of AI changes for every AI vendor in use. The changes covered are: new or default-on AI features and models; sub-processors, including underlying model providers; model deprecations and retirements; and changes to retention (including abuse-monitoring retention), residency or data-use terms. Tenant settings are adjusted, and affected profiles (BAL-8.7) and asset owners are updated, before the change reaches users of sensitive data or within a defined period no longer than the vendor's notice period. Provider-initiated model changes to assets the organization builds or configures go through change management (BAL-5.2).
evidence: List of vendor notice channels per vendor with the named owner; change log showing assessment, decision and tenant-setting change dated before the vendor's effective date; a model retirement traced to the asset owner's action.
guidance: Sources include admin message centers, sub-processor subscriptions, trust portals and deprecation pages. Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice of retirement; claude-sonnet-4-5 was deprecated on 30 Sep 2026 for retirement on 30 Nov 2026. Suggested default: assess within 10 business days and act before the effective date. Where the organization controls timing, tell affected users before the model changes. Features found already active go to inventory (BAL-1.10) and intake (BAL-1.6).

control: Unsanctioned AI use prevention and detection
requirement: Use of unsanctioned AI services, and of personal or free-plan accounts on sanctioned services, is prevented where technically possible, for example through tenant or account restrictions and the consent controls of BAL-2.6. Otherwise it is detected through network, endpoint, browser or identity telemetry, across web, desktop, extension, API and connected-app use. A record shows, for each channel, whether use is prevented, detected or not covered, and each uncovered channel has a compensating control or a BAL-1.13 exception. Monitoring is proportionate, with a documented privacy review and, where required, works-council or employee-representative review.
evidence: Channel coverage record showing prevented, detected or not covered for each channel, with gap treatments; tenant or account restriction configuration and a sample detection with its handling; privacy review, and works-council record where required, for the monitoring.
guidance: Domain blocking alone cannot tell a personal account from the enterprise tenant of the same service, so prefer tenant or account restrictions. In IBM's 2025 breach study, one in five organizations reported a breach involving shadow AI, and high shadow-AI use added about USD 670,000 to average breach cost. Endpoint discovery (BAL-1.9) and DLP coverage (BAL-4.5) feed detection. Restricting public AI web interfaces also limits their abuse as command-and-control relays (AML.T0114).

control: Shadow AI response and approved AI catalog
requirement: A published catalog lists the approved AI services, plans and models and the data classes each may process. It is derived from the BAL-8.7 profiles and referenced by the AI policy (BAL-1.1). Detected unsanctioned use triggers a defined, risk-based response (coach, restrict or block), and use involving restricted data is blocked as soon as it is detected. Every response names an approved alternative or the route to request one (BAL-1.6). Exceptions follow BAL-1.13.
evidence: Published, versioned catalog with services, plans, models and permitted data classes; response procedure stating coach, restrict and block criteria; sample of handled detections showing the response, the alternative offered and any exception reference.
guidance: Blocking alone drives circumvention: 78% of AI users bring their own tools (Microsoft Work Trend Index, 2024). Coach users at the moment of use, and reserve blocking for high-risk categories such as free plans that train on inputs and unknown agents. AI browsers and browser agent modes are blocked by default under BAL-6.20 and do not follow this graduated path. Report the unsanctioned-use trend through BAL-1.14 where implemented.

requirement: AI agents and assistants running under personal or non-organizational licenses that act on organization-owned resources (repositories, internal SaaS sessions, customer data, design files) are detected using the audit logs, tokens and sessions of those resources. Each detection is linked to the user identity, the license plan and the resources touched, so that exposure can be scoped, and is handled under BAL-8.10.
evidence: Detection rule or report using repository or SaaS audit logs to flag agent activity under personal licenses; a sample detection linked to identity, plan and resources; handling record under the shadow AI response.
guidance: In PixelLeak (Sep 2026), coding agents created public repositories under developers' personal accounts and published more than 13,000 internal screenshots from 343 organizations; 93% sat outside the organizations' own repository monitoring. Useful signals include agent user agents or commit trailers in audit logs, personal access tokens used by agent tooling, and repositories created outside the organization. BAL-5.21 sets the rule that personal-license tools are not used on organization code.

control: Supplier AI use on organization data
requirement: Suppliers that process the organization's restricted or regulated data, or data under contractual AI-use restrictions, disclose, during due diligence and at renewal, whether and how they apply AI to that data and which AI providers they use. Their contracts apply the organization's AI data-use requirements to that use: no training on the organization's data, defined retention and deletion, and advance notice before new AI use or a new AI provider is applied to that data.
evidence: Due-diligence responses on AI use and AI providers from a supplier handling restricted data; contract or addendum clauses on training, retention and notice of new AI use; register of in-scope suppliers with disclosure and contract status.
guidance: Claims administrators, law firms, outsourcers and payroll providers increasingly apply AI to entrusted data, adding model providers the organization never assessed. Flow down any AI-use restrictions the organization owes its own clients. Update legacy contracts at renewal and record gaps under BAL-1.13. The NYDFS October 2024 AI letter expects vendor due diligence to cover AI-related risks.

requirement: Each AI asset that supports a business-critical process has a documented fallback for provider outage, model retirement or a forced change of terms. The fallback is an alternate model or provider, or a manual degraded mode; it meets the process's recovery objective and is exercised at a defined interval. For assets the organization builds or configures, a replacement model passes the security release gate (BAL-5.6) before cutover; a replacement service passes the intake gate (BAL-1.6).
evidence: Fallback plan per business-critical AI asset naming triggers, alternate model, provider or manual mode, and recovery objective; record of the latest exercise and its outcome; release-gate or intake record for a replacement used at cutover.
guidance: Business criticality follows the organization's continuity classification. For other assets, record Implemented with evidence that the business-critical condition is absent, under the existing assessment rule. Model retirement is routine (Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice), and platform outages happen (AWS us-east-1, about 15 hours, Oct 2025). DORA Art. 28(8) requires documented, tested exit plans for ICT services supporting critical or important functions. Suggested default: exercise annually. Data return is covered by BAL-8.3 and grant revocation by BAL-2.7.
